META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 1.1 (8 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Core Mathematics
UNIT.content:
• Types of real numbers: natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, irrational numbers and their properties
• Number line representation of real numbers including placement of surds and irrational numbers
• Operations on real numbers: addition, subtraction, multiplication and division
• Order of operations (BODMAS/BIDMAS) applied to real numbers in multi-step computations
• Absolute value of real numbers and its applications in real-life contexts
• Reciprocals of real numbers and their use in mathematical computations
• Conversion between fractions, decimals and percentages within the real number system
• Approximation and estimation: rounding off, significant figures and decimal places
• Application of real numbers to real-life situations (e.g., temperatures in Nairobi, distances in the Rift Valley, market prices in Gikomba)
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) classify and describe types of real numbers and their properties,
b) represent real numbers on a number line,
c) perform operations on real numbers accurately,
d) determine the absolute value of real numbers and apply it in mathematical computations,
e) determine the reciprocal of real numbers and accurately apply the reciprocal of real numbers in mathematical computations,
f) apply approximation and estimation skills (rounding off, significant figures, decimal places) in real-life contexts,
g) apply real numbers in solving real-life mathematical problems,
h) appreciate the use of real numbers in day-to-day life situations.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Communication and Collaboration: the learner discusses and justifies the classification of numbers encountered in everyday Kenyan contexts — such as market prices at Gikomba market or temperatures recorded at Wilson Airport — working in pairs and groups to share reasoning about the real number system.
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: the learner evaluates, compares and operates on real numbers to solve multi-step problems drawn from real-life situations such as calculating distances between Nairobi and Mombasa or working out fair-price divisions of maize harvests in the Rift Valley.
• Self-Efficacy: the learner develops confidence in computing with real numbers — including reciprocals, absolute values and approximations — by tackling increasingly complex tasks and reflecting on their own accuracy and strategies.
• Digital Literacy: the learner uses calculators and, where available, digital devices to verify computations involving real numbers, significant figures and reciprocals, and to explore number patterns.
UNIT.values:
• Integrity: the learner records and reports computations — such as approximated measurements or market calculations — accurately and honestly, without manipulating results.
• Responsibility: the learner takes ownership of their mathematical reasoning, carefully checking operations on real numbers and acknowledging errors during peer-review activities.
• Unity: the learner collaborates respectfully with peers from diverse backgrounds during group classification and computation tasks, valuing each member's contribution to problem solving.
• Love: the learner shows care for fellow learners by offering support and explanation when peers struggle with concepts such as identifying irrational numbers or applying BODMAS to real numbers.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking Questions and Defining Problems: the learner poses questions about why certain numbers (e.g., √2, π) cannot be expressed as exact fractions, driving inquiry into the structure of the real number system.
• Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking: the learner applies order of operations, absolute value rules and reciprocal relationships to solve multi-step real-world problems, mirroring the systematic reasoning used in scientific and engineering contexts.
• Analysing and Interpreting Data: the learner interprets numerical data from Kenyan real-life contexts (e.g., rainfall figures from the Kenya Meteorological Department, population data, commodity prices) by classifying, approximating and operating on the values using properties of real numbers.
• Constructing Explanations: the learner constructs clear written and verbal explanations of why a number belongs to a particular subset of the real number system, using evidence from the number line and computation results.
UNIT.pcis:
• Financial Literacy: the learner applies operations on real numbers — including reciprocals, percentages and approximations — to real-life financial contexts such as calculating unit prices of unga (maize flour) or sukuma wiki at a Nairobi market, making change, and estimating household budgets, thereby building practical money-management skills.
• Education for Sustainable Development (Environmental Education): the learner uses real-number computations to engage with environmental data, for example approximating distances for tree-planting initiatives in Karura Forest or calculating ratios of land use in the Rift Valley, linking mathematics to sustainability.
• Life Skills (Decision Making): the learner applies estimation and approximation skills to make informed everyday decisions — such as determining whether a quoted price at the duka is a fair approximation or whether a measured quantity of githeri ingredients is within an acceptable range.
• Social Cohesion: the learner works collaboratively in diverse groups to classify numbers and solve real-life problems, fostering mutual respect and appreciation across different community backgrounds.
UNIT.careers:
• Engineering and Architecture: engineers working on infrastructure projects such as the Nairobi Expressway or LAPSSET Corridor apply real number operations, significant figures and approximations in precise calculations of measurements, loads and material quantities.
• Data Science and Actuarial Science: data analysts and actuaries at institutions like the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) or insurance companies use properties of real numbers, rational/irrational distinctions and precision in decimal representation to model financial and population data.
• Accounting and Finance: accountants and bank officers working in institutions such as Equity Bank or Kenya Commercial Bank apply reciprocals, percentages, rounding off and operations on real numbers daily in ledger computation, interest calculations and currency exchange.
• Agriculture and Agribusiness: agronomists and farmers in the Rift Valley or around Kisumu apply real-number arithmetic to calculate fertiliser ratios, land areas, crop yield estimates and fair market pricing for produce like maize, tea or beans.
• Medicine and Pharmacy: medical practitioners at Kenyatta National Hospital and pharmacists apply exact and approximate real-number computations when calculating drug dosages, body-mass indices and lab result thresholds.
UNIT.focus: This unit anchors the Grade 10 Core Mathematics Number and Algebra strand by building a rigorous yet accessible understanding of the real number system — encompassing natural numbers, integers, rationals and irrationals — and the operations, approximations and applications that flow from it. Learners engage with Kenyan real-life contexts (market prices, land measurements, temperature data and distance problems) to make the abstract structure of real numbers tangible and meaningful. The instructional approach is inquiry-based and collaborative: learners predict, investigate, explain and model their growing understanding across eight progressive lessons, each connecting back to the anchoring phenomenon of encountering numbers in everyday Kenyan life that cannot always be expressed exactly as simple fractions.
UNIT.phenomenon:
ANCHORING PHENOMENON — "The Ugali Pot Problem":

A mama mboga in Gikomba Market, Nairobi, uses a cylindrical aluminium sufuria to cook ugali for her family every evening. She knows the sufuria has a diameter of exactly 28 cm. When her daughter — a Grade 10 learner — tries to calculate the exact circumference of the pot to cut a piece of string that will fit perfectly around the rim, she multiplies 28 by π (pi). Her calculator shows 87.96459430… and the digits never end or repeat. She cuts the string to 88 cm (rounded to the nearest centimetre), but there is always a tiny gap or overlap.

What is puzzling: The diameter is a perfectly "nice" whole number — 28 cm — yet the circumference cannot be written as an exact fraction or a terminating decimal. No matter how many decimal places the calculator shows, the number goes on forever without repeating. Meanwhile, other everyday measurements — the price of a kilo of unga (Ksh 60.50), the distance from Nairobi to Nakuru (160 km), the temperature in Kisumu (34.5°C) — seem to be expressible as ordinary fractions. Why can some numbers be written exactly while others cannot? What kinds of numbers actually exist, and how do we work with them accurately in real life when we can never write them down completely?

This phenomenon propels learners to classify, represent and operate on the full system of real numbers, understand the role of approximation, and appreciate why mathematicians draw a fundamental distinction between rational and irrational numbers.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• The Maize Field Diagonal: A farmer in the Rift Valley has a perfectly square maize shamba with sides of exactly 10 metres. She wants to string a fence diagonally across the field. Using Pythagoras, the diagonal is √200 = 10√2 ≈ 14.142… metres — again a non-terminating, non-repeating decimal. Yet the side length is a "nice" number. Learners explore why √2 is irrational and where it sits on the number line relative to 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, etc.
• The Kericho Tea Estate Temperature Record: The Kenya Meteorological Department records daily minimum temperatures in Kericho. On a particular week, the recorded temperatures (in °C) are: −2.5, 0, 3, −1, 4.75, 2⅓, √3. Learners must classify each temperature as natural, integer, rational or irrational, place them on a number line, and compute the absolute differences between consecutive days to find the sharpest overnight temperature change.
• The Boda-Boda Fuel Split: Three boda-boda riders in Kisumu pool money to buy fuel. The total cost is Ksh 850. They must split the bill equally. Dividing 850 ÷ 3 = 283.333… (a repeating decimal, hence rational but non-terminating). Learners explore why this is rational (it can be written as 850/3), contrast it with irrational numbers, and practise rounding to the nearest shilling for a fair, practical split.
• The Nairobi Marathon Pace: A Kenyan marathon runner from Iten trains for the Nairobi Standard Chartered Marathon. Her target race pace is 1 km every 3 minutes and 45 seconds. Learners convert mixed units, apply reciprocals (speed = 1 ÷ time-per-km) to find km per minute, and use significant figures to compare her pace to competitors, connecting real-number operations to athletics and career contexts.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: Why can we never write some everyday numbers down completely — and how do mathematicians and Kenyan professionals work accurately with numbers that go on forever?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. What are real numbers?
2. How do we use real numbers in day-to-day situations?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1 — "What Kind of Number Is That?" (Predict & Classify)
Learners encounter the Ugali Pot anchoring phenomenon. They predict: is π a fraction? Is it a whole number? Working in pairs, they sort a set of 20 Kenyan number cards (prices, distances, temperatures, √2, π, −7, 0, 2/3, 0.333…) into groups using their own invented categories. Groups share their sorting rules. Teacher introduces the formal classification: natural numbers ⊂ integers ⊂ rationals ⊂ real numbers, and identifies irrationals. Learners revisit their cards and reclassify. DQB is opened: learners post their initial questions.

Lesson 2 — "Placing Numbers in Their Right Home" (Number Line & Representation)
Learners construct a large classroom number line (using string and pegs) spanning −5 to 5. They must physically place cards showing −√3, −1.5, 0, 2/3, √2, π − 3, 2.333…, and 3 onto the line, justifying each placement. The supporting phenomenon of the Kericho temperature record is introduced: learners plot the week's temperatures and identify which are rational vs. irrational. Learners update the DQB: "Can we always find the exact spot for an irrational number?"

Lesson 3 — "Operating on Real Numbers" (Operations & BODMAS)
Learners apply the four operations to real numbers using Kenyan market contexts (e.g., calculating total cost of ugali flour, sukuma wiki and tomatoes with mixed-number quantities). Focus on BODMAS with multi-step expressions. Pairs solve sets of increasingly complex expressions, then peer-mark using worked solutions. Common errors are surfaced and discussed. Connection back to phenomenon: "When we approximate π to compute the circumference, which operation rules still apply?"

Lesson 4 — "How Far From Zero?" (Absolute Value)
The Kericho temperature supporting phenomenon is revisited: "Which day had the biggest swing away from zero degrees?" Learners discover absolute value as "distance from zero on the number line." They work through formal definition |x|, compute absolute values of real numbers, solve simple absolute value expressions in context (e.g., |temperature change|, |profit/loss in shillings|), and represent results on the number line. DQB updated: "Does absolute value change whether a number is rational or irrational?"

Lesson 5 — "Flipping Numbers: Reciprocals" (Reciprocals & Their Properties)
The boda-boda fuel-split supporting phenomenon is introduced. Learners explore: if one rider pays 850/3 shillings, what is the reciprocal of 850/3? What does multiplying a number by its reciprocal always give? Learners derive the rule, practise finding reciprocals of integers, fractions, decimals and simple surds, and apply reciprocals in context (unit rates, speed calculations for the Iten marathon runner phenomenon). Learners test: does every real number have a reciprocal? (Discovery: zero does not.)

Lesson 6 — "Close Enough? Approximation and Significant Figures" (Rounding, S.F., D.P.)
Returning to the sufuria phenomenon: the daughter rounded 87.9645… to 88 cm. Was that wise? Learners investigate rounding to decimal places, significant figures, and when to round up vs. down in real-life contexts (drug dosages at KNH, land measurements in the Rift Valley, fuel costs). They compare the effect of rounding at different stages of a multi-step calculation (e.g., computing the total cost of fencing a maize shamba using π and √2). DQB updated: "Does rounding ever make an irrational number rational?"

Lesson 7 — "Real Numbers in Real Kenya" (Application & Problem Solving)
Learners work in groups on a structured problem-solving task that integrates all sub-strand content: a scenario in which a community water project near Lake Victoria needs to calculate pipe lengths (involving surds), water volumes (operations on decimals), cost estimates (approximation to significant figures), and equal cost-sharing (reciprocals and rational arithmetic). Each group produces a written solution with justifications. Groups present key findings to the class. Teacher facilitates sensemaking connections back to the DQB and anchoring phenomenon.

Lesson 8 — "Building Our Real Number Model" (Model Building, DQB Closure & Assessment)
Learners individually construct a cumulative visual model of the real number system: a nested Venn diagram annotated with Kenyan examples in each region, a number line showing at least one example from each sub-category, and a worked example showing how approximation, absolute value and reciprocals each appear in a single real-life Kenyan problem of their own devising. DQB is reviewed: which questions have been answered? Which remain open (pointing forward to indices and logarithms)? Lesson concludes with a class written assessment task.

LESSONS.title: What Kind of Number Is That? (Predict & Classify)

slo.purpose: This opening lesson launches the anchoring phenomenon — the Ugali Pot Problem — by surfacing learners' prior knowledge of different types of numbers and creating productive cognitive dissonance around the number π. Learners predict, sort, and begin to classify everyday numbers, discovering that some numbers cannot be written exactly, which propels the entire unit's inquiry.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (1) numbers can be classified into different types (whole numbers, fractions, decimals, and numbers like π that do not terminate or repeat); (2) the real number system contains both rational and irrational numbers; (3) everyday Kenyan measurements and quantities can be categorised within the real number system.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (1) sort a given set of numbers into 'can be written exactly' and 'cannot be written exactly' categories using reasoning; (2) represent numbers on a number line; (3) articulate in writing and speech why π presents a challenge that ordinary fractions do not; (4) pose investigative questions for the Driving Question Board.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate that: (1) mathematics is a tool for making sense of real Kenyan professional and everyday life situations; (2) asking 'what kind of number is that?' is a powerful mathematical habit of mind; (3) the inability to write certain numbers exactly is not a failure of mathematics but a profound and fascinating truth about the number system.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. What are real numbers? 2. How do we use real numbers in day-to-day situations?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 is the phenomenon-launch lesson. It drops learners into the Ugali Pot Problem, elicits their existing number intuitions through a predict-and-sort task, surfaces the central puzzle (why is 28 × π unwritable yet 28 is perfectly 'nice'?), and opens the Driving Question Board that will anchor all subsequent lessons in the unit. No formal definitions are given yet — the lesson is designed to create curiosity, not closure.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials or activities in this lesson. If physical sufuria/pots are brought to class, ensure edges are not sharp. Ensure calculators or learner digital devices are handled responsibly and returned after use.

LESSONS.overview: Learners are introduced to the anchoring phenomenon — the Ugali Pot Problem from Gikomba Market — through a short story read-aloud and a visual display of the sufuria. They first predict (without any instruction) whether a set of ten carefully chosen everyday Kenyan numbers can or cannot be written down completely and exactly. They then observe the phenomenon directly by computing 28 × π on a calculator and comparing it with 28 × 3 or 28 × 0.5, noticing the endless, non-repeating decimal. Pairs share and justify their sorting decisions, generating rich disagreement that surfaces misconceptions. The lesson closes with learners co-constructing the opening Driving Question Board (DQB), posting their most burning questions about numbers that 'go on forever'. No formal vocabulary (rational/irrational) is introduced — that is reserved for Lesson 2 — keeping this lesson firmly in the Predict and initial Observe phases.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners listen to the teacher read the Ugali Pot Problem story aloud (Gikomba Market, Nairobi; mama mboga; 28 cm sufuria; daughter's string-cutting dilemma). A large image of a cylindrical aluminium sufuria is displayed at the front. Each learner then receives a 'Number Sort Card' containing 10 numbers drawn from Kenyan everyday contexts: (1) 60.50 — price of 1 kg unga in Ksh; (2) 160 — distance Nairobi to Nakuru in km; (3) 34.5 — temperature in Kisumu in °C; (4) 1/3 — fraction of a githeri portion; (5) 0.333… — decimal form of 1/3 on a calculator; (6) √2 — diagonal of a 1m × 1m shamba plot; (7) π — ratio used in the sufuria problem; (8) 22/7 — common approximation of π; (9) 87.96459430… — calculator result of 28 × π; (10) −5 — temperature drop at the top of Mt Kenya in °C. Working individually (5 minutes), learners sort the 10 numbers into two columns on their card: Column A — 'I can write this number down completely and exactly' and Column B — 'I cannot write this number down completely and exactly'. Learners also write one sentence explaining their most puzzling choice.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Before distributing cards, read the Ugali Pot Problem story aloud slowly and dramatically, pausing after '…the digits never end or repeat.' Ask: 'Has anyone ever seen a calculator give an answer that just keeps going?' (Show of hands only — no discussion yet.) 2. Distribute Number Sort Cards face-down. Say: 'Do NOT flip the card until I say go. This is your thinking — no calculators yet, no neighbours. Trust what you already know.' 3. Say 'Go.' Set a 5-minute visible timer. Circulate silently, noting which numbers generate the most hesitation (expected: 0.333…, 22/7, √2). Do NOT correct or affirm during this phase. 4. After 5 minutes, say: 'Circle the ONE number on your card that surprised you most — the one you are least sure about.' Allow 30 seconds. 5. Cold-call exactly 4 learners (select 1 high-confidence, 1 mid, 1 struggling, 1 who circled an unexpected item): 'Amina, which column did you put 22/7 in, and why?' WAIT 12 seconds after each question before accepting a response. Do not affirm or correct — respond only with 'Interesting — does anyone have a different placement?' 6. Record on the board in two columns every placement mentioned, including contradictions, so the class can see genuine disagreement. Say: 'Hold all your placements lightly — we are about to gather some evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Elicit-Before-Explain (Predict Phase): By requiring individual written predictions before any instruction or peer discussion, the teacher surfaces genuine prior knowledge and misconceptions. Recording contradictory placements visibly on the board creates cognitive dissonance — a necessary precondition for meaningful learning. This strategy also gives the teacher instant formative data about where misconceptions cluster (typically around repeating decimals and common fractions approximating π).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Can the learner distinguish between a terminating decimal (34.5) and a non-terminating one (0.333…) at the prediction stage? (2) Does the learner place 22/7 in Column A or B — and can they articulate why? (3) Does the learner treat 87.96459430… and π as the same or different kinds of numbers? Teacher records on a clipboard the names of learners who place 1/3 and 0.333… in different columns (a key misconception to address in Lesson 3) and learners who confidently place √2 in Column B (indicating stronger prior knowledge of surds).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners now use calculators (or learner digital devices) to investigate three specific computations drawn directly from the sufuria phenomenon. Each learner records results in their exercise book under the heading 'What I Observed'. The three computations are: (A) 28 × 3 = ? (B) 28 × 0.5 = ? (C) 28 × π = ? For each result, learners answer three questions in writing: (i) How many decimal places does this answer have? (ii) Do the decimal digits form a pattern that repeats? (iii) Could you, in theory, write this number out completely on a piece of paper? After individual recording, learners compare results with a partner and mark any of the 10 Number Sort Card items they now wish to move between columns. The teacher then plays a 90-second visual: the digits of π scrolling on the board (pre-loaded: 3.14159265358979323846…) while learners watch in silence. After the scroll, the teacher asks: 'The diameter of the sufuria is 28 — a whole number. A whole number times π. Why can't the answer be a whole number, or at least a neat fraction?' Learners write a hypothesis (2–3 sentences) in their exercise books.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Before calculators are distributed, say: 'We are now gathering evidence — just like a Kenyan engineer at a construction site would gather measurements before making a decision. Record everything you see, even if it confuses you.' 2. Distribute calculators. Give 4 minutes for the three computations. Circulate and watch for learners who type 22/7 instead of the π button — gently redirect: 'Use the π key, not 22/7. Are they the same? That is actually one of our questions today.' 3. After computations, display the π digit scroll for exactly 90 seconds. Stand at the front in silence. Let the visual speak. 4. After the scroll ends, ask: 'What do you notice?' WAIT 15 seconds — a full, uncomfortable silence. Then cold-call 3 learners: 'Ochieng, what did you notice?' / 'Wanjiru, anything different from what Ochieng said?' / 'Kiprop, can you add to that?' Write their exact words on the board without paraphrasing. 5. Pose the hypothesis question: 'Why can't 28 × π be a neat fraction or terminating decimal? Write your best hypothesis — not the answer, your best current guess. 3 sentences. Go.' Allow 3 minutes of silent writing. 6. Say: 'You have just done what mathematicians do — gather evidence and form a hypothesis. We will test this hypothesis across many lessons. Do NOT erase your hypothesis — you will compare it to your thinking at the end of the unit.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence-to-Explanation Bridge (Observe Phase): The structured three-computation sequence moves learners from familiar, terminating results (28 × 3 = 84; 28 × 0.5 = 14) to the anomalous result (28 × π = 87.96459430…), making the contrast viscerally concrete. The π digit scroll is a deliberate sensory anchor — learners will remember the visual of the endless digits when the unit later formalises the definition of irrational numbers. The hypothesis-writing step initiates the explanation phase at a personal level before class-wide sensemaking begins.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Does the learner correctly identify that 28 × 3 and 28 × 0.5 terminate while 28 × π does not? (2) Does the learner's hypothesis contain any proto-mathematical language (e.g., 'it never stops', 'it has no pattern', 'you can't make it a fraction') — evidence of emerging conceptual understanding? (3) Does the learner revise their Number Sort Card placements after the calculator activity, and which items are revised? (Teacher notes revisions as evidence of responsiveness to evidence — a key scientific practice.)

framework.learnerExperience: Learners form groups of four. Each group receives a large A3 sheet with a blank two-column table (Column A: 'Can be written exactly' / Column B: 'Cannot be written exactly') and the same 10 numbers from the Number Sort Card, this time as cut-out slips. Groups physically place the slips and must reach consensus. Every placement requires a spoken justification from at least one group member — the group secretary records the justification in one sentence next to each number. Groups then rotate to view two other groups' tables (gallery walk, 3 minutes) and place a sticky dot next to any placement they disagree with. Whole-class debrief follows: teacher highlights the three most contested placements (expected: 1/3 vs. 0.333…; 22/7 vs. π; √2). Teacher introduces — for the first time — the question: 'What property would a number need to have so that you could write it down completely?' Learners write a personal response (2 sentences) before the class discusses. Teacher draws a simple two-region diagram on the board (no labels yet — just Region A and Region B) and asks learners to suggest which of the 10 numbers belongs in which region, connecting back explicitly to the sufuria: 'Where does the circumference of mama mboga's sufuria live — Region A or Region B?'
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Form groups of four deliberately (mix confidence levels). Distribute A3 sheets and cut-out number slips. Say: 'You have 8 minutes. Every number must be placed. You must agree. You must have a one-sentence reason for every placement. If you disagree, you must argue your case with evidence — not just opinion.' Set timer. 2. During group work, visit each group. Listen for: (a) confusion between 1/3 (exact fraction) and 0.333… (its decimal representation — actually the same number); (b) learners claiming 22/7 = π (a key misconception). Do NOT resolve these — instead, ask: 'Is 22/7 × 7 exactly equal to 22? What does that tell you?' WAIT 10 seconds and move on. 3. Signal gallery walk. Say: 'Walk silently. Read. Place a sticky dot on any placement you disagree with. You have 3 minutes.' 4. Return to seats. Display a tally of sticky dots on the board. Ask: 'The three most contested numbers are [name them]. Let's hear the arguments.' Cold-call 2 groups per contested number — one who placed it in A, one in B. WAIT 12 seconds per cold-call. 5. After debate, do NOT give the answer. Say: 'We do not yet have the vocabulary to settle this argument — but we will. What I can tell you is this: mathematicians did settle this argument, and it took thousands of years. By the end of this unit, you will be able to settle it in seconds.' 6. Draw the two-region diagram. Ask: 'Where does the circumference of the sufuria go?' Cold-call 1 learner. Record their answer. Say: 'We will return to this diagram in every lesson and add more detail.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Academic Controversy (Explain Phase): By requiring groups to reach consensus on contested placements and then exposing disagreements through the gallery walk, the teacher engineers productive intellectual conflict. This is more powerful than direct instruction because learners must articulate and defend reasoning, exposing the logical gaps that formal vocabulary (rational/irrational) will later fill. The two-region diagram on the board becomes the seed of the number-system model learners will develop across the unit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Can the group correctly identify that 1/3 and 0.333… represent the same number — and place them together? (2) Do learners articulate that 22/7 is a fraction (therefore 'exact' in one sense) but only an approximation of π? (3) Does the learner's written personal response to 'what property would a number need to be writable exactly?' contain the ideas of 'stopping' or 'repeating' — proto-understanding of terminating and repeating decimals? (4) During gallery walk, do learners engage critically with other groups' placements or merely observe? Teacher marks names of learners who show proto-understanding of the terminating/repeating distinction for extension follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives two sticky notes (different colours: yellow = a question I have about numbers; blue = a connection I see to real Kenyan life). Learners individually write: on yellow — their single most burning question sparked by the Ugali Pot Problem and today's activities; on blue — one Kenyan professional, job, or everyday situation where this kind of number puzzle might matter. Learners post their sticky notes on the class Driving Question Board (a large section of wall or a dedicated poster). The teacher reads aloud 6–8 yellow questions, grouping similar ones in real time. The class votes (show of hands) on the top 3 questions they most want answered by the end of the unit. These 3 questions are written in large print at the top of the DQB and will remain visible for the entire unit. The teacher then posts the unit's official Driving Question beneath the learner questions: 'Why can we never write some everyday numbers down completely — and how do mathematicians and Kenyan professionals work accurately with numbers that go on forever?'
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Distribute sticky notes. Say: 'Yellow is for YOUR questions — not questions you think the teacher wants. Real questions. Things that are actually confusing or curious to you after today. Blue is for connections — where in Kenya, in real jobs, in real life, does this number puzzle appear?' Allow 4 minutes of silent writing. 2. Circulate and read over shoulders. If a learner writes a very shallow question (e.g., 'What is pi?'), quietly prompt: 'That's a start — can you make it more specific? What about pi puzzles you most?' 3. Collect notes and post them on the DQB yourself, grouping as you go and narrating: 'Waweru asks why some decimals stop and some don't — that's in this cluster. Akinyi asks whether Kenyan engineers use π or just 22/7 — I'm putting that over here.' 4. Read 6–8 questions aloud. For each, ask: 'Who else had something close to this?' (show of hands). 5. Vote: 'Raise your hand for the question you most want answered.' Record top 3. Write them prominently. 6. Post the unit driving question. Say: 'This is the question that connects everything we will learn in this unit. Your questions and this question will guide us. We will revisit this board at the start of every lesson and at the end to see how much closer we are to an answer.' 7. Read 3–4 blue sticky notes aloud: 'Mwangi says architects designing circular water tanks in Kisumu; Fatuma says doctors measuring dosages; Omondi says GPS satellites…' Say: 'These are exactly the people who need to understand real numbers. You will meet some of their challenges in this unit.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board Protocol (DQB Phase): The DQB externalises learner curiosity and creates a public, persistent record of the class's collective inquiry. By distinguishing learner-generated questions (yellow) from real-life connections (blue), the teacher signals that both intellectual curiosity and practical application are valued equally in this classroom. Keeping the DQB visible throughout the unit allows learners to experience their own growing understanding as questions get answered — a powerful metacognitive tool aligned with CBE's emphasis on self-directed learning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Are learner questions on yellow notes specific and mathematically substantive (e.g., 'Can every fraction be turned into a decimal that eventually repeats?' 'Is there a number between π and 22/7?') or vague? Quality of questions is a direct indicator of depth of engagement with the phenomenon. (2) Do blue notes reference genuinely diverse Kenyan professional contexts, or do all learners copy one another? Diversity of contexts indicates breadth of transfer. (3) Can the learner articulate in the vote why they chose their top question — i.e., what about that question matters to them? Teacher photographs the DQB for their records and notes which question clusters dominate (this informs the sequencing emphasis for Lessons 2–6).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open a fresh double page in their exercise books labelled 'My Number Landscape — Unit Model (Start)'. They draw a large oval/blob shape representing 'All the numbers I know'. Inside the blob, they place the 10 numbers from today's Number Sort Card wherever feels right — they can cluster them, spread them, or create sub-regions if they wish. Below their diagram, they write three sentences: (1) 'Right now, I think numbers can be divided into __ types because…'; (2) 'The circumference of mama mboga's sufuria (28 × π) belongs in my diagram at… because…'; (3) 'The biggest question my diagram cannot yet answer is…'. Learners are told explicitly: 'This is your starting model. It will be wrong in some ways — that is completely fine and expected. In every lesson we will return to this page and add, move, or revise things. By Lesson 8, your model will look very different from today's version.' Learners share their model with a partner for 2 minutes, explaining one thing they are confident about and one thing they are unsure of.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Say: 'Scientists and mathematicians do not just collect facts — they build models. A model is a picture of how you currently understand something. Your model today will be incomplete. That is not a problem — it is the starting point.' 2. Give 6 minutes for individual model-drawing. Play soft background music (optional) to signal focused work time. Circulate and look for: learners who create sub-regions spontaneously (strong mathematical intuition); learners who place all 10 numbers in one undifferentiated blob (need scaffolding in Lesson 2). 3. After drawing, give 3 minutes for the three written sentences. Circulate and read sentence 3 ('biggest question my diagram cannot yet answer') — these feed directly into the DQB and inform lesson planning. 4. Signal partner share: 'Turn to your partner. You have 2 minutes. Person on the left goes first. Tell your partner one thing you are confident about in your model and one thing your model cannot yet explain.' 5. After partner share, cold-call 2 pairs: 'Njeri, what was your partner confident about?' WAIT 10 seconds. 6. Close the lesson by pointing to the DQB and the two-region diagram on the board: 'These two things — your questions on the board and your model in your book — are the most important things we produced today. Everything we learn in this unit will be building toward being able to answer those questions and complete that model. Mama mboga's sufuria will be with us the whole way.' 7. Preview Lesson 2: 'Next lesson, we will give names to the two regions in our model. Those names have been used by mathematicians for over 2,000 years. And we will find out whether 22/7 really equals π — or just pretends to.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision Protocol (Model Building Phase): The explicit instruction that 'this model will be wrong and that is fine' is pedagogically critical — it removes the fear of incorrect initial models and frames revision as the goal rather than a sign of failure. By anchoring the model to the sufuria phenomenon from the first entry, every subsequent model revision will be tied to a concrete, memorable Kenyan context. The three structured sentences force learners to articulate current understanding, make a claim about the phenomenon, and identify the frontier of their own knowledge — the three cognitive moves that drive inquiry-based learning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Does the learner spontaneously create sub-regions within their blob (e.g., separating whole numbers from decimals, or 'normal' numbers from π and √2)? This indicates readiness for formal classification in Lesson 2. (2) Is the learner's sentence 2 (where does 28 × π belong?) consistent with their Number Sort Card placement from Phase 1, or has their thinking shifted? A shift indicates genuine learning within the lesson. (3) Is sentence 3 (biggest unanswered question) mathematically substantive? Teacher collects exercise books or photographs sentence 3 from 6 representative learners (2 high / 2 mid / 2 developing) to inform the opening activity of Lesson 2.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
After the lesson, reflect on the following questions and record your responses in your professional journal:
1. PHENOMENON ENGAGEMENT: Did the Ugali Pot Problem story create genuine curiosity, or did learners seem disengaged? If disengaged, what adjustment to the story or delivery might make it more vivid or locally relevant for your specific class?
2. PREDICT PHASE DATA: Which of the 10 numbers on the Sort Card generated the most disagreement? Were the misconceptions you observed consistent with what the lesson anticipated (1/3 vs. 0.333…; 22/7 vs. π)? Note the specific names of learners who showed strong proto-understanding of the terminating/repeating distinction — plan to use them as peer-explainers in Lesson 2.
3. DQB QUALITY: Review the yellow sticky notes. Are the learner questions rich enough to sustain a unit of inquiry, or are they mostly surface-level? If mostly surface-level, consider adding a 'question stems' scaffold in Lesson 2 (e.g., 'Why does… / What would happen if… / Is it always true that…').
4. MODEL QUALITY: Review the 6 photographed sentence 3 responses ('biggest question my model cannot yet answer'). Do these questions align with the Lesson 2 content (naming rational and irrational numbers) or do they reveal a different gap that needs to be addressed first?
5. CBE COMPETENCY REFLECTION: Communication and Collaboration — did all learners participate verbally in at least one phase today, or were some silent throughout? Note the names of silent learners and plan a deliberate cold-call or pair-share role assignment for Lesson 2 to ensure their voices are heard.
6. TIMING: Note which phase ran over time and which ran short. The Explain phase (Phase 3) typically runs long due to the gallery walk debate. If time is tight, the gallery walk can be reduced to a 2-minute silent read without sticky dots, with disagreements surfaced verbally instead.

LESSONS.title: Sorting the Number World: Classifying Real Numbers from Kenyan Contexts

slo.purpose: Learners classify numbers encountered in Kenyan daily life into the formal categories of the real number system — natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rational numbers, and irrational numbers — and represent this hierarchy visually, building the conceptual foundation needed to explain why π produces an endless, non-repeating decimal when calculating the circumference of the mama mboga's sufuria.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know: (1) the definitions and distinguishing features of natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rational numbers, and irrational numbers; (2) that the real number system is structured as nested sets: ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ, with irrational numbers forming the complement of ℚ within ℝ; (3) that rational numbers can always be expressed as a ratio p/q (p, q ∈ ℤ, q ≠ 0) and produce terminating or repeating decimals; (4) that irrational numbers — such as π and √2 — cannot be expressed as such a ratio and produce non-terminating, non-repeating decimals.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (1) sort a given set of numbers into the correct subset(s) of the real number system; (2) justify their classification using mathematical reasoning; (3) represent the real number hierarchy using a nested Venn diagram; (4) place numbers accurately on a number line that includes integers, fractions, and irrational values.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate that mathematical classification is a powerful tool for making sense of the world, value precision and justification in mathematical reasoning, and show curiosity about why some numbers — like the circumference of the sufuria — cannot be written down completely.
slo.keyInquiry: What are real numbers, and how do we classify the numbers we use in day-to-day situations in Kenya?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1, learners encountered the Ugali Pot Problem and recorded initial predictions about π. In this lesson (Lesson 2 of 8), learners formally encounter the full real number system for the first time. By sorting 20 Kenyan number cards — drawn directly from the phenomenon and from familiar Kenyan life — into self-invented and then formally guided categories, learners build the conceptual vocabulary needed to precisely answer WHY the circumference of the sufuria cannot be written exactly. The lesson opens the Driving Question Board (DQB) and positions every subsequent lesson as an investigation into a specific region of the real number system.
slo.safetyNotes: No significant safety concerns for this lesson. Ensure learners handle printed number cards carefully. If scissors are used to cut printed cards, supervise use and collect scissors after the activity.

LESSONS.overview: Learners are re-anchored to the Ugali Pot Problem: the mama mboga's daughter multiplied 28 × π and got 87.96459430… — a decimal that never ends and never repeats. The lesson asks: what KIND of number is π, and how does it relate to numbers like Ksh 60.50, −7°C, or 2/3 kg of unga? Working in pairs, learners receive 20 laminated Kenyan number cards and sort them using their own invented categories (Predict + early Observe). Groups share their sorting rules. The teacher then introduces the formal real number classification — ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ, with irrationals — using a projected nested Venn diagram (Explain). Learners reclassify their cards against the formal system and place selected numbers on a class number line (Observe + Explain continued). The Driving Question Board is formally opened: each pair posts one new question that emerged from the classification activity (DQB Creation). The lesson closes with learners sketching their first individual real number hierarchy model and annotating it with at least three of their Kenyan number cards (Model Building).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are shown the phenomenon slide: the mama mboga's daughter's calculator screen displaying 28 × π = 87.96459430… alongside four other Kenyan numbers: Ksh 60.50 (price of 1 kg of unga), 160 km (Nairobi to Nakuru), −7 (overnight temperature on Mt. Kenya summit in °C), and 2/3 (fraction of a sufuria of githeri eaten). Each learner individually writes answers to three questions in their exercise books: (1) 'Write down what TYPE of number each of the five numbers is — use whatever words you already know.' (2) 'Which of these five numbers can you write down completely and exactly? Circle them.' (3) 'Is π a fraction? Yes / No / Not sure — explain your thinking in one sentence.' Learners work silently for 4 minutes. No sharing yet.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the phenomenon slide and read aloud: 'Remember our mama mboga in Gikomba? Her daughter's calculator showed 87.96459430… when she multiplied 28 by π. Look at these five numbers on the board — they all come from Kenyan daily life.' Point to each number in turn. Say: 'Before we do anything else, I want to know what YOU think. In your books, answer these three questions on your own. Do not discuss — this is your honest prediction.' Set a 4-minute timer visibly. Circulate silently, scanning written responses. Do NOT correct or comment. After 4 minutes, say: 'Keep your books open to this page — we will come back to check your predictions.' Cold-call 3 learners (one strong, one mid, one hesitant) to read ONLY their answer to question 3. After each, say: 'Thank you — hold that thought.' Allow 10 seconds of wait time after each cold-call before moving on. Record the three responses as a tally on the board: π IS a fraction / π is NOT a fraction / Not sure.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Individual written prediction (Predict-Before-Instruction). By committing predictions to paper before any instruction, learners activate prior knowledge, expose misconceptions about number types, and create a personal baseline they will revise throughout the lesson. This also gives the teacher immediate formative data on the range of prior understanding in the room.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Each learner has written a response to all three questions within 4 minutes. Teacher scans for: (a) learners who can already use terms like 'fraction', 'decimal', 'whole number', or 'integer' — these learners can be used as pair anchors; (b) learners who describe numbers only by appearance ('it has a decimal point') rather than by mathematical property — flag for targeted questioning during card sort. The tally of π IS / IS NOT / Not sure gives a whole-class snapshot of prior knowledge about irrationality.

framework.learnerExperience: Each pair receives a set of 20 laminated Kenyan Number Cards (printed and cut before the lesson). The cards include: [Natural/Whole] 1, 7, 160, 28; [Integers — negative] −3, −7, −15; [Fractions/Rationals — fractional form] 2/3, 3/4, 7/2; [Rationals — terminating decimal] 60.50, 34.5, 0.25; [Rationals — repeating decimal] 0.333…, 0.142857142857…; [Irrationals] π, √2, √3, √5; [Zero] 0. Context labels are printed on each card: e.g., '160 km — distance Nairobi to Nakuru', '34.5°C — temperature in Kisumu', '0.333… — one-third kg of unga', 'π — used to find the circumference of the sufuria', '√2 — diagonal of a 1m × 1m farm plot in Kericho'. Pairs are given 8 minutes to sort the 20 cards into groups using ANY categories they choose. They must write their group names on sticky notes and place them above their groups. After 8 minutes, three pairs share their category names (not justifications yet) with the class by reading their sticky notes aloud. Teacher records all category names on the board without evaluating them.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute card sets and say: 'You and your partner have 20 number cards. Every number on these cards comes from a real Kenyan context — prices, distances, temperatures, measurements. Your job is to sort them into groups. You choose the groups — there is no single right answer yet. You must name each group with a sticky note.' Start the 8-minute timer. Circulate actively. At each pair, crouch to eye level and ask one probing question — choose from: 'Why did you put π and √2 together?', 'What makes −7 different from 7 in your system?', 'Where does 0.333… go — and why?', 'Is 160 the same kind of number as 160.0?' Do NOT correct; only probe. After 8 minutes, cold-call 3 pairs to read their sticky-note category names. Record every category name on the board exactly as stated. Say: 'Fascinating — we have [number] different ways of grouping these numbers. Let us keep them visible. Now I am going to show you the system that mathematicians use worldwide — including Kenyan engineers, doctors, and economists.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Card Sort with Learner-Generated Categories (Elicit-Before-Tell). Learners construct their own classification schemes before the formal system is introduced. This surfaces the informal, intuitive understanding they bring (e.g., 'numbers with decimals' vs. 'whole numbers') and creates productive cognitive dissonance when the formal system challenges or refines their groupings. The Kenyan context on every card maintains direct connection to the anchoring phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) All pairs have produced at least 2 named groups within 8 minutes. (2) Pairs who have separated π and √2 from the decimal numbers show emerging awareness of the rational/irrational distinction — teacher notes these pairs for targeted questioning in Phase 3. (3) Pairs who have placed 0.333… with π show a misconception (confusing non-terminating with non-repeating) — teacher prioritises these pairs for the 'repeating vs. non-repeating' explanation in Phase 3. (4) Placement of 0 and negative numbers reveals understanding of integers and whole numbers.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher projects a large nested Venn diagram of the real number system: ℕ (natural numbers) ⊂ ℤ (integers) ⊂ ℚ (rational numbers) ⊂ ℝ (real numbers), with irrational numbers shown as the region inside ℝ but outside ℚ. Each region is colour-coded and labelled in both English and with a Kenyan example. The teacher walks through each set with its formal definition and two Kenyan examples. Learners then re-examine their 20 cards and, in pairs, re-sort them according to the formal system, placing each card in the correct region of a paper Venn diagram drawn in their exercise books. For each of four nominated cards (π, 0.333…, −7, 160), pairs must write a one-sentence justification: 'This number belongs in [set] because…'. Pairs then share justifications for π specifically — connecting directly back to the sufuria phenomenon. The class collectively constructs the answer: 'π is irrational because it cannot be written as p/q, and its decimal expansion — 3.14159… — never terminates and never repeats, which is why the daughter could never cut the string to an exact length.'
framework.teacherMoves: Project the nested Venn diagram. Say: 'Mathematicians have a precise system for classifying ALL numbers. Let me walk you through it — and I want you to check whether your sorting categories match any of these official names.' Walk through each set: NATURAL NUMBERS — say: 'These are the counting numbers: 1, 2, 3… In Kenya, when a mama mboga counts her customers — 1, 2, 3 — she is using natural numbers. Which of your cards belong here?' [Wait 10 seconds. Cold-call 1 learner.] INTEGERS — say: 'Integers include all natural numbers, zero, AND negative whole numbers. The temperature on Mt. Kenya at night: −7°C. Which cards are integers but NOT natural numbers?' [Wait 10 seconds. Cold-call 1 learner.] RATIONAL NUMBERS — say: 'A rational number is any number that can be written as a fraction p over q, where p and q are integers and q is not zero. This includes ALL terminating decimals — like Ksh 60.50 — AND all REPEATING decimals — like 0.333… Pause: is 0.333… a rational number?' [Wait 15 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners with opposing answers if available. Reveal: 0.333… = 1/3, so YES, it is rational.] IRRATIONAL NUMBERS — say: 'Now here is the crucial one. An irrational number CANNOT be written as p/q. Its decimal expansion goes on FOREVER and NEVER repeats. π is 3.14159265358979… — it never repeats. √2 is 1.41421356… — it never repeats. These numbers live OUTSIDE the rational region but still INSIDE the real number system.' Point to the sufuria image and say: 'This is exactly why the daughter could never cut the string to a perfect length. π is irrational.' Give pairs 7 minutes to re-sort cards onto their paper Venn diagrams and write the four justification sentences. Then cold-call 4 pairs — one per nominated card — to read their justification aloud. After each, ask the class: 'Do we agree? Thumbs up, thumbs sideways, or thumbs down.' Address any disagreements immediately with a direct counter-example or proof sketch.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Formal Definition Anchored to Phenomenon (Concept-Mapping + Justify-in-Writing). The formal classification is introduced AFTER learners have already attempted their own sorting, so the definitions land on fertile cognitive ground. Requiring written justifications ('This number belongs in [set] because…') forces learners to connect the formal definition to the specific number, rather than guessing by pattern-matching. Returning to the sufuria and π at the end of the phase closes the loop between abstract classification and the anchoring phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Learners correctly place all 20 cards in their paper Venn diagrams — spot-check 5 pairs' diagrams during the 7-minute work period. Key error to watch for: placing 0.333… with π (irrational) rather than ℚ (rational). (2) Written justification for π must include BOTH criteria: 'cannot be written as p/q' AND 'decimal never terminates and never repeats.' Accept either criterion alone as 'Approaching Expectations'; require both for 'Meets Expectations.' (3) Thumbs response after each cold-call justification gives real-time whole-class comprehension data. If more than one-third of learners show thumbs sideways or down after the π justification, pause and re-teach using the calculator output 87.96459430… directly.

framework.learnerExperience: Each pair is given two sticky notes. On sticky note 1, they write ONE new question that the classification activity raised for them — something they are now curious about or confused by. On sticky note 2, they write ONE thing they now understand more clearly about the sufuria problem than they did at the start of the lesson. Pairs post both sticky notes on the class Driving Question Board, which is divided into four columns: 'Questions about Rational Numbers', 'Questions about Irrational Numbers', 'Questions about How We Calculate with These Numbers', and 'Other Questions'. The teacher reads 5–6 of the posted questions aloud and clusters related questions together. The teacher explicitly marks two questions as 'We will answer this in Lesson 3' and 'We will answer this in Lesson 5', showing learners the roadmap ahead. The board remains displayed for the full 8-lesson sequence.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute two sticky notes per pair. Say: 'You have just classified 20 numbers. I want to know: what new questions does this raise for you? On your FIRST sticky note, write one question you now have — about any of the numbers, or about how we use them. On your SECOND sticky note, write one thing you now understand more clearly about the mama mboga's sufuria problem than you did 80 minutes ago.' Give 3 minutes of silent writing time. Then say: 'Come and post your sticky notes in the column that fits best. If you are not sure which column, post it in Other Questions.' Allow 2 minutes for posting. Return to the front and read 5–6 questions aloud — select questions that preview Lessons 3–8 (e.g., questions about converting fractions to decimals, about how to calculate with π, about why √2 is irrational, about rounding). After reading each selected question, say: 'This is an excellent question — write it large on the board under the relevant column.' Mark two questions with a star and say: 'We will specifically investigate THIS question in Lesson 3' and 'THIS question in Lesson 5.' Say to the class: 'This board will grow every lesson. By Lesson 8, we will have answered every question on it.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board — Question Generation and Roadmapping. The DQB serves two simultaneous sensemaking functions: (1) it externalises and validates learner curiosity, signalling that questions are a legitimate and valued product of a mathematics lesson; (2) it gives the teacher a real-time, public record of learners' conceptual gaps and emerging interests, which directly informs the design of Lessons 3–8. Publicly mapping posted questions to future lessons builds learner agency and metacognitive awareness of their own learning trajectory.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Every pair has posted at least one question sticky note within the time limit — a pair with no question is a flag for confusion or disengagement; teacher follows up individually. (2) The QUALITY of questions reveals depth of understanding: questions about surface features ('What does the symbol ℚ mean?') vs. questions about structural properties ('Can an irrational number ever be negative?') indicate different levels of conceptual engagement. (3) The 'understanding' sticky notes are collected by the teacher at the end of the lesson and reviewed to assess whether the lesson's core SLO (classify numbers into the real number hierarchy) has been achieved by the majority of learners.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner individually draws their first Real Number System Model in their exercise book. The model must include: (1) a nested Venn diagram with all five labelled regions (ℕ, ℤ, ℚ, Irrationals, ℝ); (2) at least six of the 20 Kenyan number cards placed in the correct regions of the diagram (learners choose which six); (3) one annotation connecting the model back to the sufuria: 'π belongs here because…'; (4) a title: 'My Real Number System — Lesson 2.' Learners are told: 'This model is NOT finished. You will add to it in every lesson. By Lesson 8, it will show everything we have learned about real numbers.' The teacher circulates and initials 8–10 models to confirm correct structure before the lesson ends.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'For the last 8 minutes, I want each of you to build your own model of the real number system. Open your exercise book to a fresh double page. Draw a large nested Venn diagram — big enough to write in each region. Label all five regions with their correct mathematical names and symbols. Then choose any SIX of your number cards and write them in the correct region. You MUST include π and write one sentence explaining why it is in the irrational region — connect it back to the sufuria problem.' Start the timer. Circulate and initial models that are correctly structured. If a learner has π in the wrong region, crouch and ask quietly: 'Can π be written as p divided by q where both p and q are integers? Think about the calculator screen — 87.96459430… What do you notice about those digits?' [Wait 10 seconds before offering further guidance.] With 2 minutes remaining, say: 'Write your title at the top: My Real Number System — Lesson 2. You will add to this model in every lesson. Do not close this page.' Collect exercise books from any learner whose model you have NOT initialled, for after-class review.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Individual Model Building (Progressive Model Revision). By building a personal model at the end of every lesson, learners create a visual, cumulative record of their growing understanding of the real number system. The requirement to place Kenyan number cards — including π — inside the model in every lesson maintains the direct connection to the anchoring phenomenon and prevents the model from becoming an abstract diagram divorced from the original problem. Initialling correct models during circulation provides immediate, low-stakes formative feedback.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) The nested structure is correct — ℕ inside ℤ inside ℚ inside ℝ, with irrationals in the ℝ-but-not-ℚ region. A flat (non-nested) diagram indicates the learner has not yet grasped the subset relationship. (2) π is correctly placed in the irrational region with a written justification that references either 'cannot write as p/q' or 'decimal never terminates and never repeats.' (3) All six chosen numbers are in their correct regions — errors on 0, negative numbers, or repeating decimals are the most common and should be prioritised in Lesson 3 review. Teacher reviews all un-initialled books before Lesson 3 and prepares a 3-minute 'model correction' warm-up if more than 25% of learners show structural errors.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions: (1) During the card sort (Phase 2), what were the most common learner-generated category names? Did any pairs spontaneously use the terms 'rational' or 'irrational' before instruction? This reveals the extent to which learners bring prior vocabulary from Junior School. (2) How many pairs placed 0.333… in the irrational group during the initial sort? This is the most critical misconception in this lesson (confusing non-terminating with non-repeating). If more than one-third of pairs made this error, plan a 5-minute dedicated warm-up for Lesson 3 using the long division of 1 ÷ 3 to show the repeating block. (3) Review the DQB sticky notes: do learners' questions cluster around rational numbers, irrational numbers, or operations? This should directly shape the emphasis of Lessons 3 and 4. (4) Review the 'understanding' sticky notes collected at the end of Phase 4: can learners articulate, in their own words, why the sufuria circumference cannot be written exactly? If fewer than 60% can do so, the phenomenon connection needs to be re-emphasised at the start of Lesson 3. (5) From the initialled models (Phase 5): what percentage of learners produced a correctly nested Venn diagram on the first attempt? If fewer than 70% did so, consider providing a partially pre-drawn template in Lesson 3 rather than requiring learners to construct the diagram from scratch.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners sorted 20 Kenyan number cards — including prices in Kenyan shillings, distances in km, temperatures in °C, fractions, repeating decimals, and irrational numbers such as π and √2 — into self-invented groups, then re-sorted them according to the formal real number classification system using a projected nested Venn diagram.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The real number system is organised as nested sets: natural numbers ⊂ integers ⊂ rational numbers ⊂ real numbers, with irrational numbers occupying the region inside ℝ but outside ℚ. Rational numbers can always be written as p/q and produce terminating or repeating decimals; irrational numbers — such as π and √2 — cannot be written as p/q and produce non-terminating, non-repeating decimals.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: π is an irrational number. Because it cannot be expressed as a fraction p/q, the circumference of the mama mboga's sufuria (28π cm) cannot be written as an exact decimal — the digits 87.96459430… continue forever without repeating. This is why the daughter's string always has a tiny gap or overlap no matter how many decimal places she uses.
