LESSONS.title: Lesson 3 — "Rational or Irrational? Sorting the Number Family"

slo.purpose: To deepen learners' ability to classify real numbers as rational or irrational, distinguish between terminating, recurring and non-terminating non-recurring decimals, and connect this classification to the Ugali Pot Problem phenomenon — understanding precisely why π produces a circumference that can never be written as an exact fraction.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (i) rational numbers are numbers expressible in the form p/q where p, q are integers and q ≠ 0; (ii) irrational numbers cannot be expressed as such a fraction and their decimal expansions neither terminate nor recur; (iii) together, rational and irrational numbers form the complete set of real numbers; (iv) common irrational numbers include π, √2, √3, and e; (v) everyday measurements (prices in Ksh, distances in km, temperatures) are typically rational, while geometric constants such as π arise from irrational relationships.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (i) classify a given number as rational or irrational with justification; (ii) convert a terminating or recurring decimal to a fraction; (iii) place rational and irrational numbers correctly on a number line; (iv) use a calculator to observe the decimal behaviour of numbers and draw conclusions about their classification; (v) construct a counter-example to disprove a false classification claim.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate that mathematical precision matters in real-life Kenyan professional contexts — from engineers designing water tanks in Turkana to architects drawing circular foundations in Nairobi — and that working confidently with irrational numbers requires understanding their nature rather than avoiding them.
slo.keyInquiry: What are real numbers? How do we use real numbers in day-to-day situations?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1 learners were introduced to the Ugali Pot Problem and confronted the puzzle that 28 × π produces a never-ending, non-repeating decimal. In Lesson 2 learners placed various real numbers on the number line and explored their representation. Lesson 3 now gives learners the formal classification tools to answer the puzzle directly: they investigate the decimal structure of many everyday numbers — unga prices, distances, square roots of areas — and discover that most are rational (their decimals stop or repeat), while π and √2 are provably irrational. By the end of this lesson learners can explain precisely why the sufuria circumference can never be written as an exact fraction, advancing the driving question significantly.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials are used. If physical string and a sufuria are brought to class, ensure the sufuria edges are not sharp. Calculators and mobile phones used for computation should be handled responsibly. No safety concerns beyond standard classroom practice.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by predicting whether a set of ten Kenyan everyday numbers are rational or irrational before any instruction. They then carry out a structured calculator investigation — observing the decimal expansions of numbers drawn from Kenyan market prices, distances, temperatures, and geometric constants — and sort them into a classification table. In the Explain phase the teacher formalises the definition of rational and irrational numbers using the p/q criterion, demonstrates the recurring-decimal-to-fraction conversion technique, and connects these ideas directly back to why π produces the gap in the sufuria string. Learners update the Driving Question Board with new evidence, and close by revising their cumulative real-number model to show the rational/irrational partition inside the real-number set.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives a card strip listing ten numbers drawn from Kenyan everyday life: (1) 60.5 — price of 1 kg unga in Ksh; (2) 160 — distance Nairobi to Nakuru in km; (3) 34.5 — temperature in Kisumu in °C; (4) 0.333… — one-third of a 3-litre cooking-oil bottle; (5) √4 — side of a square plot whose area is 4 m²; (6) √2 — diagonal of a 1 m × 1 m paving tile; (7) π — ratio of sufuria circumference to diameter; (8) 22/7 — the fraction a carpenter uses to approximate π; (9) 0.142857142857… — 1 ÷ 7 on a calculator; (10) √5 — a measurement arising in a right-triangle roof truss design. Learners work individually for 5 minutes, sorting each number into one of three columns in their exercise books: 'Definitely can write as a fraction', 'Definitely CANNOT write as a fraction', 'Not sure'. Learners then share predictions with a shoulder partner for 2 minutes. No feedback is given yet.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute card strips as learners settle. Say: 'Before we do any mathematics together, I want to know what you already think. Look at these ten numbers — all of them appear in Kenyan everyday life. Sort them silently into the three columns. You have 5 minutes. Go.' Circulate and observe — do NOT correct. After 5 minutes say: 'Now share your sorting with your partner. Convince them where you placed each number and why.' After pair-share, cold-call 4 learners (choose one who placed √2 as 'fraction', one who placed 0.333… as 'cannot', one uncertain about 22/7, one uncertain about 0.142857…). Record their predictions visibly on the board in a class tally. Say: 'We are not judging right or wrong yet. By the end of today you will be able to defend every one of these placements with mathematical evidence.' Leave predictions visible throughout the lesson.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-then-Investigate (Elicitation of Prior Knowledge): surfacing misconceptions before instruction allows the teacher to target instruction precisely. Learners who incorrectly place 0.333… as 'cannot write as fraction' reveal a gap between recognising fractions and recognising recurring decimals as fractions — a key sensemaking moment to address in Phase 3.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher observes sorting patterns during circulation. Key indicators: (a) most learners correctly identify 60.5, 160, 34.5 as rational — if not, prior number-sense needs revisiting; (b) learners who place 22/7 and π in the same column reveal a crucial misconception to address; (c) the proportion of 'not sure' responses for √2 and √5 signals readiness level for the irrational number concept.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in pairs. Each pair has a scientific calculator (or a mobile phone calculator). They receive a structured observation worksheet titled 'Decimal Detective'. For each of the ten numbers on their card strip they: (a) enter the number into the calculator and record the full display; (b) describe the decimal pattern in one sentence (e.g., 'stops after 1 decimal place', 'same 6 digits repeat forever', 'never stops, no pattern I can see'); (c) attempt to write the number as a fraction p/q — or write 'I cannot find any fraction that equals this exactly'. For numbers 1–3 and 5 and 8 this is straightforward. For number 4 (0.333…) learners discover 1/3 by reasoning. For numbers 6, 7, 10 learners observe the non-terminating non-repeating display and attempt — and fail — to find an exact fraction. The teacher then shows, using a projected calculator, that 22/7 = 3.142857142857… (repeating) while π = 3.14159265358979… (no repetition visible across all displayed digits). Learners record this critical difference in red pen in their worksheets. The observation closes with each pair writing one sentence: 'We think the key difference between Group A numbers and Group B numbers is…'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You are now going to be decimal detectives. Your job is to look very carefully at what your calculator shows and describe what you see — like a scientist recording an observation, not jumping to conclusions yet.' Allow 15 minutes for calculator investigation. Circulate — pause at pairs who may think 22/7 = π and ask: 'Enter 22 ÷ 7 on your calculator. Now enter π directly. Look at the digits after 3.14 — are they identical?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Cold-call 2 pairs to share what they notice. Then project a large calculator display at the front showing both: 22/7 = 3.142857142857142857… versus π = 3.14159265358979323846… Say: 'A Kenyan architect in Nairobi and a mama mboga in Gikomba both use 22/7 as an approximation for π. Is 22/7 actually equal to π?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] Cold-call 3 learners. Then say: 'Write the key difference you observe in red — this is the most important observation of today.' After pairs write their sentences, cold-call 3 pairs to share. Record key phrases on the board.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data Collection and Pattern Recognition (NGSS Science and Engineering Practice 3 — Planning and Carrying Out Investigations; Practice 4 — Analysing and Interpreting Data): learners act as empirical investigators, using the calculator as a measurement instrument. The deliberate juxtaposition of 22/7 (repeating decimal, therefore rational) against π (non-repeating, therefore irrational) is the pivotal observational moment that directly answers why the sufuria string always has a gap — because no fraction can ever equal π exactly.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check worksheets for: (a) correct decimal descriptions for all 10 numbers — especially that 0.142857142857… is described as 'repeating' not 'random'; (b) pairs who correctly attempt 1/3 for 0.333… are ready for the formal conversion technique; (c) pairs who write 'the repeating ones can be fractions, the non-repeating ones cannot' in their summary sentence have independently arrived at the core classification criterion — affirm this publicly.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher delivers a structured explanation in three blocks, each followed by a learner practice task. BLOCK 1 (10 min) — Formal Definitions: The teacher writes the definition of a rational number (p/q, integers, q ≠ 0) and an irrational number on the board. Learners copy and then immediately classify all 10 card-strip numbers using the formal definition, revising their Phase 1 predictions. BLOCK 2 (10 min) — Converting Recurring Decimals to Fractions: Teacher demonstrates the algebraic method using 0.333… → let x = 0.333…, then 10x = 3.333…, subtract: 9x = 3, so x = 1/3. Learners practise with 0.142857142857… (= 1/7) and 0.181818… (= 2/11). BLOCK 3 (8 min) — Back to the Phenomenon: Teacher explicitly connects to the sufuria problem. Learners write a 'phenomenon connection sentence': 'The circumference of the sufuria (28π cm) cannot be written as an exact fraction because π is irrational, which means ___.' They complete the sentence and share with their partner.
framework.teacherMoves: BLOCK 1: Write definition on board and say: 'A rational number is any number that can be written in the form p over q, where p and q are integers and q is not zero. An irrational number is a real number that CANNOT be written in this form — its decimal expansion never terminates and never repeats.' Point to the class prediction tally still on the board. Ask: 'Using this definition, look at your Phase 1 tally — who needs to move a number?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Cold-call 3 learners to justify a reclassification. Target learner who placed √4 as irrational — ask: 'What is √4 exactly?' [WAIT 8 seconds.] Establish √4 = 2 = 2/1, therefore rational. BLOCK 2: Say: 'Now I am going to show you a mathematical trick that reveals why recurring decimals are rational — they ARE fractions in disguise.' Work through 0.333… on the board step by step. Then say: 'Your turn. Work out whether 0.142857142857… is rational using the same method.' [WAIT 15 seconds for individual attempt.] Cold-call 1 learner to the board. Affirm and then say: 'This is exactly why your calculator shows 1 ÷ 7 as a repeating decimal — it is rational.' BLOCK 3: Ask: 'So — back to Gikomba Market. The sufuria has a diameter of exactly 28 cm. The daughter multiplies by π. Why does she ALWAYS get a gap or overlap when she cuts the string?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Cold-call 2 learners. Then say: 'Complete this sentence in your book: The circumference cannot be written as an exact fraction because…' After 3 minutes, cold-call 3 learners to read their sentence aloud. Correct any conflation of π and 22/7.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Formal Definition Anchored to Prior Observation (NGSS Practice 6 — Constructing Explanations): learners move from empirical pattern observation (Phase 2) to formal mathematical language. The recurring-decimal-to-fraction conversion is a concrete procedural bridge that makes the abstract p/q definition tangible. The phenomenon reconnection in Block 3 ensures the formal language serves the driving question rather than existing in isolation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit check after Block 1: scan 6 learner books to confirm √4 = rational is now corrected. After Block 2: the board work by the cold-called learner for 0.142857… is visible to all — correct any algebraic errors publicly. After Block 3: listen to the three read-aloud sentences. A complete sentence must include: (i) the word 'irrational', (ii) a reference to the decimal expansion not terminating or repeating, and (iii) the implication for exact measurement. Sentences missing any element flag learners for targeted follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board. The DQB has three columns: 'What we observed', 'What we now understand', 'New questions we have'. Working in groups of four, learners write new sticky notes for each column based on today's lesson. Suggested contributions: 'Observed' — '22/7 and π look similar on a calculator but have different decimal structures'; 'Understand' — 'π is irrational because its decimal never terminates or repeats — so no string length can be exactly right'; 'New questions' — 'Are there other irrational numbers in Kenyan building and cooking? Can we prove √2 is irrational?' Groups post their notes and the teacher facilitates a 5-minute gallery walk where learners place a star sticker on the most insightful 'New question' note from another group.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'It is time to update our Driving Question Board. Remember our question: why can we never write some everyday numbers down completely? You now have new evidence and new understanding. In your groups, write at least one sticky note for each column. You have 5 minutes.' Circulate and prompt groups who are stuck with: 'What was the most surprising thing your calculator showed you today?' After posting, say: 'Do a quick gallery walk — read the other groups' notes and place a star on the new question you find most mathematically interesting.' After the gallery walk, cold-call 2 learners to read the starred questions aloud. Acknowledge and say: 'These questions will drive Lessons 4 and 5 — we will investigate surds and the proof that √2 is irrational.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Collaborative Knowledge Consolidation via DQB (NGSS Practice 7 — Engaging in Argument from Evidence; Practice 8 — Obtaining, Evaluating and Communicating Information): the DQB externalises the class's collective growing understanding. The gallery walk with star stickers creates peer evaluation of questions, building metacognitive awareness of what is still unknown — a key competence in the CBE framework.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads all sticky notes during circulation. Quality indicators: 'Observed' notes should reference specific decimal evidence (not vague impressions); 'Understand' notes should use the word 'irrational' or 'rational' correctly; 'New question' notes reveal depth of curiosity — questions about proof of irrationality indicate high-level thinking. Photograph the board for reference in planning Lessons 4–5.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve the cumulative real-number model they began in Lesson 1 (a large set diagram in their exercise books). In Lesson 1 they drew the outer set 'Real Numbers'. In Lesson 2 they added a number line inside it. Today they add the key structural partition: they draw two non-overlapping subsets inside the Real Numbers set, label one 'Rational Numbers (Q)' and one 'Irrational Numbers'. Inside the Rational Numbers subset they place examples from today: 60.5, 160, 34.5, 1/3, 22/7, 0.142857… = 1/7, √4 = 2. Inside the Irrational Numbers subset they place: π, √2, √3, √5. They annotate each irrational number with a one-phrase note explaining its decimal behaviour. They also add a small inset sketch of the sufuria with the label '28π cm — irrational circumference' with an arrow pointing to the Irrational Numbers subset. Learners share their model with a partner and give one piece of feedback using the stem: 'I notice you placed ___ in ___. I agree/disagree because…'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your cumulative model from Lessons 1 and 2. Today we are adding the most important structural feature of the real-number system. Draw two non-overlapping regions inside your Real Numbers set. Label them Rational Numbers — using the symbol Q — and Irrational Numbers. Now place every number from today's card strip into the correct region and annotate.' Allow 8 minutes. Circulate and look for: learners who leave √4 in Irrational Numbers (address immediately by asking 'What is the exact value of √4?'); learners who place π and 22/7 in the same region (redirect to their Phase 2 calculator observation). After 8 minutes say: 'Share your model with your partner. Give feedback using the sentence stem on the board: I notice you placed blank in blank — I agree or disagree because blank.' Allow 4 minutes for peer feedback. Close by cold-calling 2 learners to describe their model to the class, emphasising the sufuria annotation. Say: 'Every lesson we will add one more layer to this model. By Lesson 8 it will be a complete map of the real number system — and it will answer our driving question fully.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (NGSS Practice 2 — Developing and Using Models): the set diagram is a living scientific model that learners revise lesson by lesson. Adding the rational/irrational partition today is the single most structurally important revision in the 8-lesson sequence because it establishes the fundamental topology of the real number system. Anchoring the sufuria in the irrational subset makes the model a direct answer-in-progress to the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect 6 exercise books at random at the end of the lesson. Check: (a) the two subsets are drawn as non-overlapping and both inside Real Numbers; (b) all 10 card-strip numbers are placed correctly; (c) irrational numbers each carry a decimal-behaviour annotation; (d) the sufuria annotation is present. Any book missing (b) or (d) indicates a learner who has not yet connected the classification to the phenomenon — flag for one-on-one follow-up at the start of Lesson 4.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did learners independently arrive at the repeating-vs-non-repeating distinction in Phase 2, or did most need the projected calculator comparison? If most needed the projection, design a more guided observation worksheet for the next cohort. (2) How many learners still conflated 22/7 with π after the Block 3 explanation? This is a persistent and important misconception in Kenyan classrooms — if more than 25% of learners still conflate them, plan a brief 5-minute consolidation activity at the start of Lesson 4. (3) Did the DQB 'New Questions' column generate genuine curiosity about proof and surds? If questions were thin or repetitive, consider introducing a 'mathematical mystery card' stimulus in Lesson 4 — e.g., a short story about a Kenyan engineer who could not use an exact value for √2 when designing a diagonal roof beam. (4) Were learners able to give substantive peer feedback on the cumulative model, or was it superficial? If feedback was weak, model a high-quality feedback exchange explicitly at the start of the next peer-review activity. (5) Note the names of learners whose Phase 1 predictions were most accurate — these learners may be strong peer-teachers for differentiated grouping in Lesson 4.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners observed the decimal expansions of ten Kenyan everyday numbers on a calculator and discovered that some decimals terminate (60.5), some repeat in a pattern (0.142857142857… = 1/7; 0.333… = 1/3; 22/7 = 3.142857…), and others — particularly π and √2 — neither terminate nor repeat across all visible digits.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Learners learned that rational numbers are expressible as p/q (integers, q ≠ 0), that terminating and recurring decimals are always rational, that irrational numbers have non-terminating non-repeating decimal expansions, and that π is irrational — which is exactly why multiplying the sufuria's diameter (28 cm) by π produces a circumference that can never be written as an exact fraction or a terminating decimal.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The formal classification of real numbers into rational and irrational subsets, the algebraic technique for converting a recurring decimal to a fraction, and the direct connection between π's irrationality and the unavoidable gap or overlap when cutting a string to fit the sufuria rim were explained and practised.

LESSONS.title: Placing Numbers on the Line: Can We Always Find the Exact Spot?

slo.purpose: Learners physically construct a classroom number line and place rational and irrational numbers on it, justifying each position using decimal approximations and benchmark reasoning, thereby deepening their understanding of how all real numbers — including non-terminating, non-repeating ones — occupy precise (if unwriteable) locations on the number line.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (1) every real number — rational or irrational — corresponds to exactly one point on the number line; (2) irrational numbers such as √2, √3 and π can be approximated to any desired degree of accuracy to locate them; (3) temperature readings and other everyday Kenyan measurements can be classified as rational or irrational; (4) the number line is a complete, continuous model of the real number system with no gaps.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (1) estimate the decimal value of simple surds (√2 ≈ 1.414, √3 ≈ 1.732) and expressions such as π − 3 ≈ 0.1416 using a calculator or known benchmarks; (2) order a mixed set of real numbers and place them correctly on a scaled number line; (3) justify the placement of each number using mathematical reasoning; (4) classify a set of real-world Kericho temperature data as rational or irrational.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate that: (1) mathematical precision and physical reality sometimes require careful approximation; (2) irrational numbers are not 'broken' or 'incomplete' — they have exact positions even when they cannot be written exactly; (3) collaborative reasoning and respectful debate sharpen mathematical justification skills.
slo.keyInquiry: Can we always find the exact spot for an irrational number on the number line — and what does that tell us about the kind of number the ugali-pot circumference really is?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–3 learners identified and classified rational and irrational numbers and explored non-terminating decimals. In this lesson (4 of 8) learners make the abstract number line concrete: they stretch a real string across the classroom (mimicking the daughter's string around the sufuria rim) and must physically peg irrational numbers like √2 and π − 3 onto it. This bridges classification (what kind of number is it?) to representation (where exactly does it live?), directly answering why the daughter's string always has a tiny gap — 88 cm is a peg placed slightly off the true irrational position. The Kericho temperature subplot grounds the classification skill in a second real Kenyan context.
slo.safetyNotes: When stretching the string number line across the classroom, ensure the string is held at a safe height (below neck level, approximately waist height) and is secured at both ends before learners move around it. Scissors used to cut number cards should be handled with care. Learners with mobility difficulties should be assigned card-holding or recording roles at a fixed station.

LESSONS.overview: Learners collaborate to construct a large physical number line spanning −5 to 5 using string and pegs strung across the classroom. Working in groups, they receive eight number cards (−√3, −1.5, 0, 2/3, √2, π − 3, 2.333…, and 3) and must estimate, debate, and physically peg each card to its correct position on the line, providing a written justification. The lesson is anchored by returning to the Ugali Pot Problem: the daughter's string (88 cm) is itself a 'peg' placed near — but not exactly at — the irrational circumference. A second supporting phenomenon, the Kericho Tea-Country Temperature Record, is introduced: learners receive a table of seven daily temperatures from Kericho and must plot these on a mini number line strip, classifying each as rational or irrational. The lesson closes with a Driving Question Board update focused on the new question: "Can we always find the exact spot for an irrational number?"

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives a slip showing the eight numbers: −√3, −1.5, 0, 2/3, √2, π − 3, 2.333…, and 3. Without a calculator, learners individually sketch a mini number line from −5 to 5 in their exercise books and mark where they think each number belongs, writing a one-sentence justification for each placement. They then compare predictions with a partner, noting any disagreements before the whole-class share.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the eight number cards on the board in random order. Say: 'Before we touch any string or calculator, I want your best guess for where each of these numbers lives on a number line from −5 to 5. Use what you already know — benchmarks, what you remember about π, square roots, fractions. Sketch it yourself first — 3 minutes, silent, pencils only.' Set a visible 3-minute timer. After 3 minutes: 'Now turn to your elbow partner. You have 90 seconds — find ONE number you disagree about and explain why.' After partner talk, cold-call 4 pairs (select one strong, one mid, two uncertain based on prior lesson exit tickets): 'Amina and Brian — which number did you disagree about and what were your two positions?' WAIT 12 seconds after each pair responds before probing. For each response ask: 'What number did you use as a benchmark to decide that?' Do NOT confirm or correct yet — record disagreements on the board in a 'We disagree about…' column. Close by returning to the phenomenon: 'Remember the daughter cutting string for the sufuria rim — she had to decide where to cut. Today we are doing exactly that, but with a number line instead of a pot.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Benchmark Anchoring Prediction: learners use known reference points (0, 1, −1, 2, integers) as anchors to estimate unfamiliar values. This activates prior knowledge about the relative magnitude of surds and π before formal computation, and surfaces misconceptions (e.g. learners who place √2 at 2 or π − 3 near 0.5) that the Observe phase will address.
framework.formativeAssessment: Circulate and photograph 3–4 learner mini number lines. Look for: (1) Does the learner correctly place 0 and integers as anchors? (2) Is −√3 placed to the left of −1? (3) Is π − 3 placed between 0 and 1? Flag learners who place all irrationals at integer positions — these learners need targeted support in Phase 3. Record names for cold-calling in Phase 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4 receive: a set of 8 laminated number cards, a calculator, a 'Decimal Approximation Table' worksheet (two columns: Number | Decimal approximation to 4 d.p.), and a Kericho Temperature Record card showing 7 days of temperatures (e.g. 18°C, 19.5°C, √5 °C above baseline [≈2.236°C above], 20°C, 18.75°C, 21°C, 19.333…°C). Groups first complete the Decimal Approximation Table for all 8 number-line cards using their calculators. They then examine the string number line (already stretched across the classroom, marked with tape at every integer from −5 to 5 and subdivided at every 0.5) and peg each card to what they believe is the correct position. Groups must also classify each of the 7 Kericho temperatures as rational or irrational and plot them on a printed mini number-line strip (16°C to 23°C). The teacher circulates but does not confirm placements — groups record their decimal approximations and initial peg positions on the worksheet.
framework.teacherMoves: Before releasing groups: 'Your job in the next 18 minutes is two things. First: fill in the Decimal Approximation Table — every number to 4 decimal places. Second: peg your 8 cards onto the class number line. But — here is the rule — before you peg, your group must agree on a justification sentence: WHY does this number go here? Write it on the back of the card.' Assign roles within each group: Calculator Operator, Peg Placer, Justification Writer, Kericho Temperature Analyst. Circulate every 3 minutes. At each group, ask ONE targeted question — do NOT answer questions about placement: 'You've placed π − 3 there — what decimal did your calculator give you? Where is that between on the number line?' and 'For √3 — is it bigger or smaller than 1.5? How do you know?' At the 10-minute mark, call attention: 'Kericho Temperature Analysts — have you found any irrational temperatures in that data? What makes you say that?' WAIT 10 seconds. At the 15-minute mark, ring a bell: 'Peg Placers — step back from the line. Look at the whole class line together. Do all groups agree on where 2.333… is sitting? Look carefully.' Allow 2 minutes of silent inspection before Phase 3.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Physical Embodied Modelling: the act of pegging a card to a real string makes the abstract density of the real number line tangible. Learners must commit to a physical location, creating productive cognitive dissonance when groups place the same number in slightly different positions. The Kericho temperature subplot uses a familiar Kenyan context (Kericho tea-country weather) to reinforce that the classification skill transfers beyond the sufuria.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the Decimal Approximation Tables as you circulate: (1) Can learners correctly compute √2 ≈ 1.4142 and √3 ≈ 1.7321? (2) Do learners recognise π − 3 ≈ 0.1416 (not 0.5 or 3.14)? (3) For the Kericho data, do learners identify √5 above baseline as irrational and 18.75 = 75/4 as rational? Flag any group that places 2.333… between 2 and 2.25 — this suggests they do not recognise 2.333… = 7/3 ≈ 2.333. Note this for the Explain phase. Take a photo of the full class number line before Phase 3 for reference.

framework.learnerExperience: The class gathers around the string number line. Each group defends ONE assigned card's placement (teacher assigns so that stronger groups get the irrational numbers). The defending group reads their justification sentence aloud. The rest of the class acts as a 'Mathematical Court' — they may challenge the placement with evidence (a different decimal approximation, a benchmark argument) or support it. After all 8 cards are defended and finalised, learners complete a 'Number Type Gallery' in their books: a table with columns for Number | Decimal Form | Rational or Irrational? | Exact position knowable? | How the daughter's string problem connects. They then revisit the Ugali Pot Problem: 'The daughter's calculator showed 87.9645… She pegged her string at 88 cm. On our class number line, show me — with your finger — the tiny gap between 88 and the true irrational value π × 28.' Teacher leads a whole-class discussion connecting irrational placement to the sufuria string gap.
framework.teacherMoves: Open Phase 3: 'We have a number line full of pegged cards. Some may be in the wrong place. We are going to hold a Mathematical Court. Each group will defend one card — then the court decides: keep it or move it, and why.' Assign cards: Group 1 → −√3; Group 2 → π − 3; Group 3 → 2.333…; Group 4 → √2; remaining cards (−1.5, 0, 2/3, 3) defended by volunteers. For each defence, prompt the defending group: 'State your decimal approximation. State two numbers it falls between. State your justification.' WAIT 12 seconds after each defence before opening to the court. Cold-call at least 2 challengers per card from different groups. For irrational placements, push with: 'You said √2 is approximately 1.4142. Can you write it exactly? If not, how do you KNOW it belongs exactly there and not one millimetre to the right?' WAIT 15 seconds — this is the key productive struggle moment. After all 8 cards are settled, transition to the phenomenon connection: 'Now think about the daughter and the sufuria. Her calculator said 87.9645… — she cut at 88. On the number line of circumferences, is 88 exactly at the irrational point π × 28? What does the tiny gap represent in real life?' Cold-call 3 learners. Validate answers: the gap is real, it matters in engineering and cooking, and it is WHY mathematicians developed approximation techniques. Close: 'For the Kericho temperatures — Analyst groups, which temperature was irrational and how did you know?' Cold-call 2 groups. Confirm that √5 above a baseline is irrational because √5 is irrational, while 18.75, 19.5, 20, 21 are all rational.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Mathematical Court Argumentation (SEP: Engaging in Argument from Evidence): learners construct and evaluate claims about number placement using decimal evidence. This mirrors how engineers and scientists justify measurements — you cannot write the exact value, but you can prove your approximation is better than an alternative. Connecting back to the sufuria gap makes the abstraction meaningful: the 'wrong' peg position costs the daughter a small but real piece of string.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for three specific things during defences: (1) Does the learner cite a decimal approximation as evidence (not just 'it looks about right')? (2) Does the learner correctly distinguish 'I can approximate it' from 'I can write it exactly'? (3) For 2.333… — do learners recognise it as rational (= 7/3) even though it is non-terminating? Learners who say 2.333… is irrational because 'it goes on forever' need immediate targeted questioning: 'Does it repeat? What fraction equals 2.333…?' This is the most common misconception at this stage and must be addressed before Lesson 5.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually write one sticky note (or card) to add to the class DQB. The prompt has two parts: (A) 'Something I can now answer about the driving question that I couldn't answer in Lesson 3:' and (B) 'A new question the number line activity raised for me:' Examples of expected new questions: 'Can we ever run out of irrational numbers between two rationals?', 'Is there a number that is neither rational nor irrational?', 'How did mathematicians first prove π goes on forever?', 'Does every point on the number line have a number, or are there gaps?' The teacher reads out 5–6 contributions aloud, clusters them on the DQB under two headings ('What we now know' and 'What we still wonder'), and explicitly connects the new anchoring question 'Can we always find the exact spot for an irrational number?' to the DQB.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute sticky notes. Say: 'You have 4 minutes. On your sticky note, write TWO things: first, one thing about our driving question you can now answer better after today's number line activity — and second, one new question today raised for you. Write your name small in the corner.' After 4 minutes, collect notes, read 5–6 aloud (choose a spread of ability levels). As you read each: 'Does anyone want to add to this thought?' WAIT 10 seconds. Sort notes onto the DQB in real time. Point to the 'What we still wonder' cluster and say: 'Look at how many new questions one number line raised. This is what mathematics feels like — every answer opens three doors. Our driving question asks why we can never write some numbers down completely. Today you proved that those numbers still have a home — a precise spot — on the number line. That is extraordinary.' Point to the sufuria photograph on the wall (if displayed): 'The daughter's string landed at 88. The true spot for π × 28 is just to the left of that. Always. No matter how many decimal places her calculator shows.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Collaborative Knowledge Mapping on the DQB: clustering learner-generated questions publicly shows the class that mathematical understanding is cumulative and that new knowledge creates new questions rather than closing inquiry. This metacognitive strategy helps learners see their own growth across the 8-lesson sequence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Read all sticky notes before the next lesson. Count: (1) How many learners correctly state that irrational numbers have exact positions even if unwriteable? (2) How many learners still conflate non-terminating with irrational (mentioning 2.333… as irrational)? (3) What proportion of new questions are about density of irrationals vs. about computation? Use this to calibrate the opening of Lesson 5.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their cumulative 'Real Number System Model' (a diagram started in Lesson 1 showing nested sets: Natural → Whole → Integer → Rational → Real, with Irrational as the complement of Rational within Real). They now annotate it with three new additions: (1) They draw a number line inset on their model, marking the approximate positions of √2, −√3, π − 3, and 2.333… with dotted arrows showing 'irrational' vs. 'rational' landing zones. (2) They add a speech bubble to the 'Irrational' region: 'These numbers have exact positions on the number line even though we can never write them completely.' (3) They add a 'Kenyan Connections' box listing: sufuria circumference (π × 28), Kericho temperature anomaly (√5 above baseline), alongside known rational examples (unga price Ksh 60.50 = 121/2, Nairobi–Nakuru distance 160 km = 160/1). Groups briefly share their updated models with a neighbouring group, explaining one new annotation each.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute learners' individual model sheets (collected at the end of Lesson 3). Say: 'Your model of the real number system needs an upgrade. In the next 8 minutes, add three things — I will write them on the board.' Write the three additions clearly. Circulate and look specifically at the 'Kenyan Connections' box: 'Tell me — why is 60.50 rational? Can you write it as a fraction?' WAIT 12 seconds. 'Why is the sufuria circumference irrational? What about 160 km?' Push learners to articulate: 'It's not about whether it's big or small — it's about whether it equals a ratio of two integers.' After 8 minutes, ask groups to share with neighbours: 'Explain one annotation to your neighbour — they must be able to tell me what you added and why, so make it clear.' Close the lesson: 'Your model now shows that the real number line has no gaps — every number, rational or irrational, has a home. But can we always find that home precisely? That question goes onto our DQB and drives our next lesson, where we explore operations with irrational numbers.' Collect models for teacher review.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Progressive Model Revision (SEP: Developing and Using Models): learners iteratively refine their nested-set diagram to incorporate the number line dimension. Adding the 'Kenyan Connections' box grounds the abstract model in local reality and reinforces transfer — the skill of classification applies to sufuria measurements and Kericho temperatures alike, not just textbook examples.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect models at the end of the lesson. Check three things: (1) Is the number line inset correctly annotated — are irrational numbers placed in the correct region relative to integers? (2) Is the speech bubble mathematically accurate (exact position vs. exact written form)? (3) Does the 'Kenyan Connections' box correctly classify all listed examples? Any learner who classifies 160 km as irrational (because 'it is a measurement') needs a targeted discussion at the start of Lesson 5 distinguishing measurement imprecision from mathematical irrationality.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions and record brief notes: (1) PLACEMENT ACCURACY — When groups pegged their cards to the string number line, how accurate were the irrational placements compared to the rational ones? What does this suggest about learners' comfort with decimal approximation? (2) THE 2.333… MISCONCEPTION — Did learners initially classify 2.333… as irrational because it is non-terminating? How many? Did the Mathematical Court discussion resolve this, or do you need to revisit the 'repeating = rational' rule explicitly in Lesson 5? (3) KERICHO TEMPERATURES — Did learners engage authentically with the Kericho data, or did it feel like an add-on? Would a different Kenyan context (e.g. Rift Valley rainfall data, Kisumu lake temperature) have been more resonant for your specific class? (4) PHENOMENON CONNECTION — During the sufuria gap discussion in Phase 3, were learners able to articulate WHY the gap exists (irrational circumference vs. rational cut)? If not, consider beginning Lesson 5 with a 2-minute re-enactment using an actual piece of string and a circular object. (5) DQB QUALITY — What new questions appeared on the DQB that you had not anticipated? Do any of these questions open a productive thread for Lessons 5–8 (operations with irrationals, rationalising denominators, limits of approximation)?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners constructed a classroom string number line (−5 to 5) and pegged 8 number cards (including −√3, √2, π − 3, 2.333…) to their correct positions after computing decimal approximations. They also plotted and classified 7 Kericho daily temperatures as rational or irrational on a mini number-line strip.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Every real number — whether rational or irrational — occupies a unique, precise point on the number line. Irrational numbers like √2 and π − 3 cannot be written exactly as fractions or terminating decimals, but they can be located to any desired accuracy using decimal approximations. Non-terminating repeating decimals (e.g. 2.333…) are rational. The daughter's 88 cm string is a rational approximation pegged near — but never exactly at — the irrational circumference π × 28.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The real number line is complete and continuous: between any two rational numbers there are infinitely many irrational numbers, and every irrational number has a definite address on the line even though we can never write that address in full. This is why the ugali-pot daughter's string always has a tiny gap — she is placing a rational peg at an irrational address, and no matter how many decimal places her calculator shows, she can only get closer, never exact.

LESSONS.title: Operating on Real Numbers — Can We Calculate Exactly with Numbers That Never End?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: operations on real numbers, BODMAS, irrational number arithmetic, approximation, surds

slo.purpose: Learners apply the four operations and BODMAS to real numbers — including integers, fractions, decimals, and surds — and investigate what happens to rational and irrational numbers when they are combined, in order to advance understanding of why the sufuria's circumference can never be computed exactly.
slo.knowledge:
• The four operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) can be applied to all real numbers.
• BODMAS (Brackets, Of/Orders, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction) governs the order of operations for real numbers.
• The sum, difference, or product of two rationals is always rational; combining a rational with an irrational generally produces an irrational; but some combinations of irrationals can be rational (e.g. √2 × √2 = 2).
• Approximation introduces small but unavoidable errors; working with the exact symbolic form (e.g. 28π) preserves precision.
slo.skills:
• Apply BODMAS correctly to multi-step calculations involving integers, fractions, decimals, and irrational numbers.
• Decide, with justification, whether the result of combining two real numbers will be rational or irrational.
• Choose an appropriate level of approximation for a given real-life context (e.g. cutting string, pricing unga, measuring temperature).
slo.attitudes:
• Appreciate that mathematical precision matters in everyday Kenyan professional contexts — from construction in Nairobi to pharmacy dosage calculations.
• Show perseverance and care when working with non-terminating numbers, recognising that keeping the symbolic form is often more accurate than premature rounding.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use real numbers in day-to-day situations?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1–4 established what real numbers are and where they live on the number line. Lesson 5 now asks: what happens when we operate on them? Learners discover that arithmetic on real numbers follows consistent rules (BODMAS), but that the rational/irrational character of results depends on which types of numbers are combined — directly explaining why 28 × π cannot be 'simplified away' into a nice fraction and why the daughter will always face a gap or overlap when she cuts her string.
slo.safetyNotes: No specific hazards. If physical string and a sufuria are used as props, ensure the sufuria rim has no sharp burrs.

LESSONS.overview:
This lesson is the operational heart of the Real Numbers sequence. Having classified, represented, and located real numbers on the number line in Lessons 1–4, learners now compute with them. The lesson opens by returning to the anchoring phenomenon: the daughter calculated 28 × π on her calculator and got 87.96459430…. She rounded to 88 cm and cut her string — but there was always a tiny gap or overlap. The central question driving this lesson is: does it matter in what order we do calculations with real numbers, and what kind of number do we get when we mix rationals and irrationals?

Learners begin with a prediction task — estimating, without a calculator, whether combining specific pairs of Kenyan-context numbers (e.g. the price of unga plus the cost of charcoal; the circumference of the sufuria minus a rational approximation) will yield a rational or irrational result. They then work through a structured guided-inquiry activity using real Kenyan marketplace and construction contexts to discover the closure and combination rules for real number operations, and to apply BODMAS in multi-step calculations that include surds and π.

The lesson closes with learners revising the class model of the real number system to annotate it with operation results: arrows showing 'rational + rational = rational', 'rational × irrational = irrational (usually)', and 'irrational × irrational = sometimes rational'. This cumulative model directly feeds the next lesson on indices and standard form, and keeps the sufuria phenomenon alive as the running thread.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives a half-sheet with six 'Number Pairs' drawn from Kenyan contexts (see below). Without using a calculator, they write R (rational) or I (irrational) to predict whether the result of the stated operation will be rational or irrational, then share their prediction with a partner using a Think-Pair-Share. The six pairs are: (1) 60.50 + 34.5 [price of unga + temperature in Kisumu in °C]; (2) π + 3; (3) √2 × √2; (4) 28 × π [the sufuria circumference]; (5) (1/3) ÷ (2/3); (6) √3 + √5. Learners record their reasoning in one sentence per pair.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the half-sheets face-down. Say: 'Before we calculate anything today, I want your gut feeling. You have 3 minutes — silent, individual thinking first. Flip your sheet.' [Allow 3 minutes of silent work.] After 3 minutes: 'Now turn to your partner — 90 seconds each to compare answers. If you disagree, write down WHY you disagree.' [Allow 3 minutes pair discussion.] Cold-call 4 learners (aim for mixed confidence levels): 'Amina, what did you predict for pair 4 — the sufuria one — and why?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds after posing each question before accepting a response.] After each response, ask the class: 'Hands up if you agreed with Amina. Hands up if you disagreed.' Do NOT confirm or correct answers yet. Write the six predictions on the board in a T-chart: PREDICT: Rational | PREDICT: Irrational. Say: 'We are going to test every one of these predictions today. Keep your sheet — you'll revise it at the end.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Activate-and-Surface (Elicitation): By surfacing predictions before instruction, the teacher makes prior conceptions visible. Disagreements — especially on pairs 3 (√2 × √2 = 2, which is rational and surprises most learners) and 4 (28 × π, irrational) — create productive cognitive conflict that the Observe Phase will resolve. Recording predictions publicly on a T-chart creates accountability and makes later revision meaningful.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans the room during silent work: are learners writing reasoning or just guessing R/I? Target indicator: learner can articulate at least one reason (e.g. 'both are fractions so it stays a fraction'). Listen during cold-calls for misconceptions: if learners claim √2 × √2 is irrational, note this for targeted instruction in the Explain Phase. If more than half the class predicts pair 4 is rational, flag this as the central misconception to address.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of 4 on a structured 'Calculation Station' worksheet with three sections. Section A (BODMAS warm-up, 3 questions): e.g. 'A mama mboga in Gikomba charges Ksh 60.50 for a 2 kg packet of unga and Ksh 15.00 for 500 g of sukuma wiki. She also gives a discount of Ksh 5.25. Calculate the total cost without a calculator, showing all steps in BODMAS order.' Section B (Combining number types, 4 questions): learners compute (i) 1/4 + 0.75, (ii) π + 3, (iii) √2 × √2, (iv) 28 × π — writing the exact symbolic answer AND a decimal approximation to 4 d.p. for each. Section C (Pattern hunt, 1 question): 'Look at your four answers in Section B. Make a conjecture: what determines whether your answer is rational or irrational?' Groups record their conjecture as a full sentence.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute worksheets. Say: 'Section A is a BODMAS workout — show every step, no steps skipped. Section B is the investigation: write both the exact form AND the decimal. Section C is your detective work — what pattern do you see?' [Allow 12 minutes of group work.] Circulate actively, targeting these check-ins: (1) At every group, look at Section B part (iii): if they wrote √2 × √2 = √4 = 2 correctly, ask 'Is 2 rational or irrational?' [WAIT TIME: 10 seconds]. (2) For Section B part (iv), ensure groups write '28π' as the exact form — not just the decimal. If a group writes only '87.9646', say: 'You have the approximation — brilliant. But what is the EXACT answer? How would a mathematician write it?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds.] (3) At the halfway point, cold-call one group: 'Kamau's group — read me your conjecture from Section C so far.' After they respond, ask the class: 'Does anyone have a different conjecture?' Cold-call 2 more groups. Do not validate yet. At the end of group work, ask all groups to hold up their Section C conjecture sentence for a gallery walk (30-second silent read of neighbours' conjectures).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Inquiry with Evidence Recording: The three-section worksheet scaffolds learners from familiar BODMAS practice (Section A) into novel territory (Section B) and then into pattern recognition (Section C). Writing both exact and decimal forms side-by-side in Section B forces learners to confront the difference between an approximation and an exact answer — directly mirroring the daughter's situation with 28π vs 87.96 cm. The gallery walk surfaces diverse conjectures without premature teacher closure.
framework.formativeAssessment: Key observable: in Section B, can learners correctly identify √2 × √2 = 2 (rational)? This is the highest-leverage misconception. If 3 or more groups get it wrong, plan a whole-class pause during the Explain Phase. In Section C, look for conjectures that mention 'type of number' or 'whether π or √ is involved' — these show readiness for the formal rule. Conjectures that only mention 'size of numbers' indicate the learner is not yet thinking about number classification.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher leads a whole-class debrief structured around four 'result cards' posted on the board (one per Section B question). For each card, a group representative states their answer; the class votes; the teacher confirms and annotates. Learners then receive a short reference note (one side of A5) titled 'Rules for Combining Real Numbers' with four rules stated in plain language plus one symbolic example each. Learners immediately apply these rules to three new 'Nairobi context' problems: (1) A jua kali fabricator in Kamukunji needs to cut a steel rod of length (3 + √5) metres into two equal pieces — is each piece rational or irrational? (2) A pharmacist in Kericho measures two doses: 0.333… litres and 1/6 of a litre of a syrup — what is the total, and is it rational? (3) The daughter recalculates the sufuria rim: she uses 22/7 instead of π — is 28 × 22/7 rational or irrational, and why does this matter for her string? Learners write answers individually, then compare with a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Post the four result cards. For each: 'Group 2 — Wanjiru, read your answer for question (iii).' [WAIT TIME: 10 seconds.] 'Class — thumbs up if you agree, thumbs sideways if you're not sure, thumbs down if you disagree.' Count responses visibly. For √2 × √2 = 2: say 'This one surprises a lot of people. Let's see why it's rational.' Write on the board: √2 × √2 = (√2)² = 2. Say: 'Two irrational numbers can multiply to give a rational number. This is NOT what most of us predicted.' Pause for effect. Distribute the reference note. Read through the four rules aloud together. Then say: 'Three application problems — I want SILENT individual work for 4 minutes first, then you compare with your partner. Go.' [4 minutes silent, then 2 minutes pair comparison.] Cold-call on problem 3: 'Odhiambo — if the daughter uses 22/7 instead of π, is 28 × 22/7 rational or irrational?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds.] After the answer, say: 'So by switching to 22/7, she made the calculation rational — she got exactly 88 cm. But wait — is 22/7 actually equal to π?' [WAIT TIME: 10 seconds.] 'No — it is only an approximation. So she introduced an error in exchange for being able to write the answer down. That is the trade-off at the heart of our driving question.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with Counter-Example Emphasis: Each application problem is framed as a claim to justify (rational or irrational?) with evidence (the calculation) and reasoning (which rule applies). The √2 × √2 counter-example is treated as a 'surprise result' deliberately — research shows that counter-intuitive cases deepen schema revision. The problem about 22/7 explicitly reconnects to the phenomenon and surfaces the precision-vs-exactness trade-off that is the driving question's core tension.
framework.formativeAssessment: For problem 3, the target indicator is: learner can state both that 28 × 22/7 = 88 (rational) AND that 22/7 ≠ π, therefore the answer is an approximation, not exact. If learners say only '88, rational' without noting the approximation issue, probe: 'Is 22/7 the same as π?' This reveals whether the learner has integrated the lesson's core idea. Collect half-sheets at end of Explain Phase — scan for correct application of all four rules.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group receives two sticky notes of different colours: one ORANGE ('Something we can now answer about the driving question') and one BLUE ('A new question this lesson raised for us'). Groups discuss for 90 seconds, then a representative posts both notes on the class DQB under the driving question banner: 'Why can we never write some everyday numbers down completely — and how do mathematicians and Kenyan professionals work accurately with numbers that go on forever?' The class does a 2-minute silent gallery walk reading all new notes. The teacher then highlights two orange notes and two blue notes aloud, connecting them explicitly to the lesson's findings.
framework.teacherMoves: Hand out sticky notes. Say: 'Orange note: what can we NOW answer about our big question that we couldn't before today? Blue note: what new question did today's lesson raise for you? You have 90 seconds as a group.' [90 seconds group discussion.] 'One representative — post both notes on the DQB. Everyone else: stand up and do a silent gallery walk for 2 minutes. Read what other groups wrote.' [2 minutes silent gallery walk.] After gallery walk, teacher reads two orange notes aloud: e.g. 'Group 3 says: we can now answer WHY the daughter always gets a gap — because 28 × π is irrational and can never be written exactly, no matter how many decimal places.' Say: 'Exactly. That is a real answer to our driving question.' Then read a blue note: e.g. 'Group 1 asks: can computers store π exactly?' Say: 'That is a beautiful new question. Does anyone want to take a guess before next lesson?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds. Cold-call 2 volunteers.] Close by pointing to the DQB: 'Look at how much ground we have covered since Lesson 1. We predicted, we classified, we placed numbers on the line, and now we operate on them. Each lesson, our model gets richer.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Two-Colour DQB Protocol: Using two distinct note colours forces learners to distinguish between resolved understanding and emergent questions, preventing the DQB from becoming a mere display. The gallery walk ensures every learner reads peers' thinking, not just their own group's. The teacher's act of reading and validating specific notes models metacognitive reflection — showing that both 'answers' and 'new questions' are valued outcomes of scientific and mathematical inquiry.
framework.formativeAssessment: Quality indicator for orange notes: does the note reference the phenomenon (the sufuria, the daughter, 28π) or use correct mathematical vocabulary (rational, irrational, approximation)? Vague notes like 'we learned about BODMAS' indicate surface processing. Quality indicator for blue notes: does the question push forward into territory not yet covered (e.g. indices, surds, infinite series) or reveal a residual misconception? Collect blue notes at the end — they directly inform Lesson 6 planning.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve the cumulative class model of the real number system — a nested-set diagram (ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ, with ℝ∖ℚ labelled as irrationals) built across Lessons 1–4. Working individually in their exercise books, each learner adds an 'Operations Layer' to their personal copy of the model: four annotated arrows showing what type of number results when each operation is performed between: (i) rational + rational, (ii) rational + irrational, (iii) irrational + irrational, (iv) irrational × irrational. They label the sufuria calculation (28 × π) on their model with an arrow from 28 (in ℚ) and π (in ℝ∖ℚ) pointing to 28π (in ℝ∖ℚ) — annotated: 'Exact answer — irrational. Approximate answer 88 cm — rational.' They add one sentence at the bottom: 'Today's lesson changes my understanding of the driving question because…'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Get out your personal model from your exercise book — the nested diagram we have been building since Lesson 1. Today we add the Operations Layer.' Display the class model on the board. 'I want four arrows on your diagram. Each arrow starts at two numbers — one on each side — and points to what type of number the result is. Use the rules from your reference note.' [Allow 4 minutes of individual model revision.] Circulate. If a learner is only writing labels without arrows, say: 'Show me the journey — where do 28 and π live in your diagram, and where does 28π land?' [WAIT TIME: 10 seconds.] After 4 minutes: 'Now write your one sentence at the bottom. Finish the stem: Today's lesson changes my understanding of the driving question because…' [Allow 90 seconds.] Cold-call 3 learners to read their sentences. [WAIT TIME: 10 seconds per learner.] After each, ask the class: 'Does anyone want to add to what Njeri said?' Close: 'Your model now shows not just the number families, but how they behave when you combine them. Next lesson, we will zoom in on a special family of real numbers — those written as powers — and see what new tools that gives us for the sufuria problem and beyond.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (Iterative Modelling): The model is not created fresh each lesson but deliberately built up over the sequence, making the growth of understanding visible and tangible. Adding the 'Operations Layer' as arrows (rather than static labels) foregrounds the dynamic, relational nature of number classification — numbers don't just exist in categories, they interact across categories. The sentence stem 'Today's lesson changes my understanding because…' is a metacognitive forcing function that consolidates lesson-level learning into the larger storyline arc.
framework.formativeAssessment: Target: learner's model correctly shows that rational × irrational → irrational (with 28 × π as the example) AND that irrational × irrational can be rational (with √2 × √2 = 2 as the example). If both are present, the learner has grasped the lesson's conceptual core. Sentence stems are collected or photographed as an exit indicator — look for explicit reference to the driving question tension (exact vs approximate) rather than just restating 'we learned BODMAS'. Students who write only procedural sentences (e.g. 'I now know how to do BODMAS') should be targeted for a brief check-in at the start of Lesson 6.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
1. During the Predict Phase, which of the six number pairs generated the most disagreement, and what does that tell you about your learners' residual misconceptions about rational vs irrational numbers going into Lesson 6?
2. Were learners able to write '28π' as an exact symbolic answer, or did most groups jump straight to the decimal approximation? If the latter, what instructional move could you use in Lesson 6 to reinforce the value of exact symbolic forms?
3. The application problem about 22/7 vs π is designed to surface the precision trade-off at the heart of the driving question. Did learners articulate both parts of the answer (28 × 22/7 = 88 is rational AND 22/7 ≠ π, so it is an approximation)? If not, how will you revisit this in the next lesson?
4. Looking at the blue sticky notes from the DQB, what new questions did learners raise? Do any of these questions connect to upcoming content in the Real Numbers sub-strand (e.g. indices, surds, standard form), and can you use them as an entry point for Lesson 6?
5. How rich were the 'Operations Layer' additions to learners' personal models? Did the models show arrows and relational thinking, or just static labels? What scaffolding might help weaker learners make their models more dynamic before the next lesson?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners computed the results of adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing pairs of real numbers drawn from Kenyan marketplace and construction contexts (unga prices, the sufuria circumference, pharmacist doses in Kericho, jua kali fabrication in Kamukunji). They observed that most combinations follow predictable rules — but that irrational × irrational can sometimes yield a rational result (√2 × √2 = 2), and that replacing π with 22/7 makes the sufuria calculation rational but introduces an approximation error.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The four operations on real numbers obey BODMAS. When two rationals are combined by any operation (result defined), the result is always rational. When a rational is combined with an irrational by addition or subtraction, the result is always irrational. When a rational is multiplied or divided by an irrational, the result is generally irrational. When two irrationals are combined, the result can be either rational or irrational — there is no single rule. Keeping the exact symbolic form (e.g. 28π) is more precise than any decimal approximation.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The daughter's calculator shows 87.96459430… because 28 × π is the product of a rational (28) and an irrational (π), making the result irrational — a number that cannot be written as a terminating or repeating decimal, no matter how many digits the calculator displays. When she rounds to 88 cm or uses 22/7 instead of π, she converts the answer into a rational number — gaining the ability to write it down exactly — but at the cost of introducing a small error. This is why there is always a tiny gap or overlap in her string: exactness and writability are fundamentally in tension for irrational numbers.
